articles.title: Sau sự cố hố ga rò rỉ khiến nước thải chảy thẳng ra biển, Gia Lai chi 3,5 tỷ đồng xử lý
articles.text:
TPO - Gia Lai đầu tư 3,5 tỷ đồng xây trạm bơm, đường ống dẫn nước thải từ khu vực Nhơn Lý về trạm xử lý Suối Cả nhằm giúp giảm tải hệ thống hiện hữu, cải thiện vệ sinh môi trường.
Ngày 12/10, UBND tỉnh Gia Lai cho biết, đã phê duyệt chủ trương đầu tư dự án Trạm bơm và tuyến ống thu gom, dẫn nước thải khu vực Nhơn Lý về Trạm xử lý nước thải Suối Cả (phường Quy Nhơn Đông). Dự án có tổng vốn đầu tư 3,5 tỷ đồng, triển khai trong giai đoạn 2026-2027.
Dự án được đầu tư nhằm thu gom, chuyển một phần nước thải sinh hoạt khu vực Lý Hưng - Lý Lương về Trạm xử lý nước thải Suối Cả với lưu lượng phù hợp khả năng tiếp nhận, xử lý của trạm. Qua đó, góp phần giảm tải cho Trạm xử lý nước thải Lý Lương công suất 100m³/ngày đêm, khai thác hiệu quả công trình đã được đầu tư và cải thiện vệ sinh môi trường khu vực Nhơn Lý.
Nước từ hố ga rò rỉ chảy tràn lên mặt đường. Ảnh: Trương Định.
Theo quy mô được phê duyệt, dự án sẽ xây dựng trạm bơm nước thải mới với công suất dự kiến khoảng 200m³/ngày đêm, cùng hệ thống đường ống thu gom và ống áp lực dẫn nước thải về Trạm xử lý nước thải Suối Cả.
Đối với Trạm xử lý nước thải Suối Cả hiện hữu, có công suất thiết kế 170m³/ngày đêm, dự án sẽ lắp đặt lại các thiết bị cần thiết và tổ chức vận hành thử nghiệm trong 3 tháng. Quá trình này nhằm đánh giá khả năng tiếp nhận, xử lý nước thải, hoàn thiện các thủ tục môi trường theo quy định và bảo đảm hệ thống vận hành đồng bộ sau khi đấu nối.
Trước đó, như Tiền Phong đã phản ánh, đầu tháng 7/2026, nhiều hố ga trên tuyến đường ven biển thuộc phường Quy Nhơn Đông liên tục rò rỉ, khiến nước thải trào lên mặt đường, bốc mùi hôi nồng nặc, ảnh hưởng đến sinh hoạt của người dân và du khách.
Nước thải chảy thẳng ra biển. Ảnh: Trương Định.
Theo lãnh đạo UBND phường Quy Nhơn Đông, hệ thống ban đầu được thiết kế để thu gom nước mưa. Tuy nhiên, sau đó được đấu nối thêm nước thải sinh hoạt để dẫn về trạm xử lý.
Việc tiếp nhận thêm lượng nước thải khiến hệ thống quá tải, trong khi đường ống có kích thước nhỏ, dẫn đến hiện tượng nước dội ngược và tràn ra ngoài qua các hố ga. Toàn tuyến có 27 hố ga, trong đó 6 hố ga bị rò rỉ. Đến nay, địa phương đã cơ bản khắc phục tình trạng nước thải tràn lên mặt đường và chảy ra biển.
Xây dựng cơ sở dữ liệu đất đai "đúng, đủ, sạch, sống" đang là nhiệm vụ trọng tâm. Sự kết hợp giữa công nghệ viễn thám, thiết bị bay không người lái (UAV) và trí tuệ nhân tạo không gian địa lý (GeoAI) đang trở thành "chìa khóa" giúp ngành chức năng tối ưu hóa công tác kiểm tra, đối soát và làm sạch dữ liệu trên phạm vi toàn quốc.
TPO - Trong quá trình thăm dò nền đất chuẩn bị xây nhà tại khu tái định cư Cửa Bạc, phường Hoa Lư, tỉnh Ninh Bình, một người dân bất ngờ phát hiện nhiều hiện vật bằng sành xếp chồng dưới lòng đất. Qua giám định ban đầu, các hiện vật được xác định có niên đại thời Trần, khoảng thế kỷ XIII-XIV.
TP - Từ những cụm máy tính hiệu năng cao đến các mô hình ngôn ngữ, tác nhân AI có thể tham gia vận hành doanh nghiệp, trí tuệ nhân tạo đang mở ra một cuộc đua mới trong giới công nghệ Việt. Các doanh nghiệp không chỉ tìm cách ứng dụng AI, mà còn đầu tư hạ tầng, phát triển sản phẩm và tìm đường đưa năng lực công nghệ Việt ra thị trường toàn cầu.
TPO - Chiều nay (12/10), Viện Hàn lâm Khoa học Hoàng gia Thụy Điển quyết định trao Giải Nobel Kinh tế năm 2026 cho 2 nhà kinh tế học người Mỹ Robert Hall và Michael Woodford, với công trình về “nền tảng kinh tế vi mô của chính sách ổn định kinh tế vĩ mô”, giúp nền kinh tế giảm bớt thăng trầm.
TPO - Sau khoảng 45 ngày được bảo vệ, 57 cá thể rùa biển con nở tại đặc khu Phú Quý, tỉnh Lâm Đồng được lực lượng kiểm ngư cùng người dân thả về môi trường tự nhiên.
UAV Cobra 600 kết hợp tên lửa IRIS-T tạo nên ‘taxi tên lửa’ tự hành độc đáo, mở ra kỷ nguyên mới cho hệ thống phòng không châu Âu với tầm đánh chặn vượt trội và chi phí tối ưu.
TPO - Trong quá trình làm rẫy, ông Thái Văn Diệu (trú xã Vũ Quang, Hà Tĩnh) phát hiện một cá thể gà lôi trắng nặng 2,5kg nên đã thông báo và giao nộp cho lực lượng chức năng.
TPO - Sau các trận mưa lớn kéo dài, ở nhiều nơi trên địa bàn phía Tây tỉnh Gia Lai liên tiếp xuất hiện các vị trí sụt lở, nứt toác. Mới đây tại thôn Chư Ty 4, xã Đức Cơ xuất hiện vết sụt lở khủng khiếp, trải dài hàng cây số.
TP - Hơn một thế kỷ trước, những thân cây khổng lồ ở Taipingshan (Núi Thái Bình) được xem là tài nguyên quý giá, những đoàn tàu nhỏ ngày đêm đưa gỗ ra khỏi núi. Ngày nay, đường ray cũ, rừng già và suối nước nóng lại trở thành sức hút đưa du khách đến vùng núi Nghi Lan, Đài Loan (Trung Quốc).
TPO - Trong bối cảnh AI được sử dụng ngày càng phổ biến trong hoạt động của chính phủ số, các chuyên gia đến từ Pháp cho rằng, Việt Nam cần sớm thành lập một Uỷ ban quốc gia về đạo đức AI, như cách tiếp cận của một số nước.
TPO - Những chai nhựa, bìa cứng, lon bia… được người dân Đà Nẵng phân loại và thu gom để đổi lấy hạt giống tại Ngày hội “Hải Vân xanh – Sáng tạo – Số hoá – Tuần hoàn”. Hoạt động góp phần đưa lối sống xanh, tái chế và kinh tế tuần hoàn đến gần hơn với cộng đồng.
TPO - Kỷ nguyên AI mang đến bước nhảy vọt về hiệu suất học tập, nhưng cũng đặt giảng đường trước một câu hỏi lớn: Sinh viên đang dùng AI để học tốt hơn hay đang để AI học thay? Khi những bài làm điểm cao có thể xuất xưởng chỉ sau vài câu lệnh, làm sao để đo lường năng lực thật của người học? Tại tọa đàm do Báo Tiền Phong và Trường ĐH Giao thông vận tải TP.HCM tổ chức, các chuyên gia cảnh báo nguy cơ người trẻ bị ru ngủ bởi đáp án sẵn có.
TPO - Đối thoại Quy Nhơn về khí hậu và chuyển đổi (gọi tắt Đối thoại Quy Nhơn) lần thứ nhất quy tụ hơn 100 đại biểu cấp cao trong nước và quốc tế, hướng tới kết nối khoa học, chính sách, tài chính và doanh nghiệp, tìm kiếm giải pháp ứng phó biến đổi khí hậu gắn với phát triển bền vững.
TPO - Một đàn voọc chà vá chân nâu vừa được ghi nhận xuất hiện tại đỉnh Bạch Mã, nơi có độ cao hơn 1.400 m thuộc Vườn Quốc gia Bạch Mã (xã Phú Lộc, TP. Huế).
TPO - Tại Diễn đàn Đô thị Thông minh Tương lai, các chuyên gia, cơ quan quản lý, doanh nghiệp cho rằng, sự phát triển của thành phố thông minh sẽ đến giai đoạn đô thị vận hành bằng tác nhân AI, nơi các tác nhân AI vận hành xuyên suốt các dịch vụ công và dịch vụ thương mại thực tế theo bộ quy tắc chung.
TPO - Đà Nẵng xây dựng Đề án truyền thông khoa học công nghệ, đổi mới sáng tạo và chuyển đổi số giai đoạn 2026-2030, hướng đến hệ thống truyền thông đồng bộ, đa nền tảng, lấy hiệu quả tiếp cận công chúng làm trọng tâm.

articles.title: Popular weight loss drugs linked to a surprising fingernail problem
articles.text:
Popular weight loss drugs linked to a surprising fingernail problem
Scientists have uncovered a surprising link between popular GLP-1 weight loss drugs and nail detachment, hair loss, and scalp inflammation.
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- Beyond
- Summary:
- Popular GLP-1 weight loss drugs, such as Ozempic and Wegovy, have been linked to unexpectedly high rates of nail detachment, hair loss, and scalp inflammation, with some problems occurring several times more frequently among users. Researchers found that weight loss alone could not fully explain the differences, suggesting there may be more to these overlooked symptoms.
- Share:
Popular GLP-1 medications used for weight loss and type 2 diabetes (such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound, Victoza, and Trulicity) have been linked to an unexpected problem involving fingernails. A multinational study found that people taking these drugs were more than four times as likely to report nail detachment, a condition in which the nail separates from the skin underneath it.
Researchers found that 39% of GLP-1 users experienced nail detachment, compared with just 9% of people who had never taken the medications. Nail discoloration was also considerably more common, and two-thirds (66%) of users reported at least one nail disorder.
The findings, presented at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) Congress 2026, come from the first controlled study to investigate the possible relationship between GLP-1 medications and nail health.
Unexpected Nail Problems Among GLP-1 Users
GLP-1 receptor agonists have become increasingly popular for managing obesity and type 2 diabetes. These medications act on a hormone signaling system that helps regulate blood sugar and appetite, making them effective tools for improving metabolic health and supporting weight loss.
However, scientists are still investigating their potential effects on other parts of the body. Until recently, information about nail changes during GLP-1 treatment came primarily from individual reports of possible adverse reactions, rather than controlled comparisons.
To investigate the connection, researchers examined 575 people using GLP-1 medications and compared them with 1,329 individuals who had type 2 diabetes and/or obesity but had never used the drugs. Participants were recruited from France, the United States, Brazil, and Mexico.
The results revealed a consistent pattern. Overall, 66% of GLP-1 users reported at least one nail disorder, compared with 53% of the control group. Nail discoloration showed an especially large difference, affecting 46% of users versus 17% of nonusers.
Nail detachment was even more striking, with reports more than four times as common among those taking GLP-1 medications.
Weight Loss Alone May Not Explain the Nail Changes
One important question was whether the nail problems might simply be related to weight loss, rather than to the medications themselves. Rapid changes in body weight can affect nutrition and other physiological processes, potentially influencing nail and hair health.
However, the researchers found that weight loss did not fully account for the differences. Even when they limited their analysis to participants who had lost weight, GLP-1 users continued to report significantly more nail problems than those who had not used the medications.
"Until now, nail changes associated with GLP-1 therapies had essentially been anecdotal," said study author Dr. Charles Taïeb. "Our findings show a clear association, but they also underline an important point: not everything that happens during GLP-1 treatment is necessarily caused by the treatment itself."
The researchers emphasized that their findings do not prove that GLP-1 drugs cause nail disorders. Approximately half of the medication users said they had experienced nail problems even before beginning treatment.
When the researchers accounted for existing skin conditions and nutritional deficiencies, some of the differences between the groups became smaller. Nevertheless, nail detachment and discoloration remained approximately two to three times more common among GLP-1 users after these adjustments.
Scientists Also Find Higher Rates of Hair Loss and Scalp Problems
The unexpected findings were not limited to fingernails.
A companion study examining the same participants identified significant differences in hair and scalp health among people taking GLP-1 medications.
Half of GLP-1 users reported unusual hair loss, compared with 34% of nonusers. Reduced hair volume or density was also substantially more common, affecting 42% of users versus 19% of the control group.
Researchers additionally examined hair loss that began after treatment started. This was reported by 26% of GLP-1 users, compared with 12% of nonusers, making it more than twice as common in the medication group.
Scalp redness was approximately three times more frequent among GLP-1 users.
A particularly interesting finding was that hair loss rarely appeared by itself. Most users who reported shedding also experienced other scalp symptoms, including itching, redness or flaking skin.
These accompanying symptoms raised the possibility that inflammation could be contributing to the changes, rather than the hair loss being explained entirely by rapid weight reduction.
"This suggests that what is happening on the scalp may go beyond the classical shedding seen after rapid weight loss and involve an inflammatory component," explained study author Dr. Bruno Halioua. "Scalp inflammation was the rule rather than the exception, which clinicians do not currently look for and which may be treatable. Taken together, our findings suggest that factors beyond weight loss alone may contribute to the hair, scalp and nail changes observed among GLP-1 users."
What the Findings Mean for People Taking GLP-1 Drugs
Despite the relatively high frequency of reported symptoms, the researchers stressed that the findings should encourage awareness rather than alarm.
"These changes are frequent, usually benign, and are not a reason to stop an effective treatment on one's own initiative," he said. "Anyone who notices hair shedding, an itchy or red scalp or nail changes should mention it to their doctor rather than discontinue therapy."
There are also important limitations to consider. Both investigations were cross-sectional studies, meaning they examined participants' experiences without following them over time to establish how symptoms developed. The findings also relied on symptoms reported by participants rather than standardized clinical examinations.
As a result, the studies can reveal patterns and associations, but they cannot determine whether GLP-1 medications directly caused the reported nail, hair, or scalp problems.
To investigate these questions more thoroughly, the research team plans to conduct prospective studies that follow patients from the beginning of treatment. These investigations will include standardized skin, hair and nail examinations along with biological monitoring.
The goal is to establish when the changes first appear, identify the mechanisms behind them, and determine whether they improve or disappear over time.
The research received institutional support from DUCRAY Laboratories (Pierre Fabre Group), a company specializing in dermatological and hair care products developed to help manage skin and scalp conditions and improve quality of life.

articles.title: Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice
articles.text:
Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- PLOS
- Summary:
- Scientists discovered that declining levels of a protein called Menin may help drive aging, and restoring it in older mice reversed several age-related changes in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing with a simple amino acid called D-serine improved memory and learning, offering a potential new approach to age-related cognitive decline.
- Share:
What if some of the changes we associate with aging begin with the loss of a single protein deep inside the brain? Scientists investigating that possibility found that restoring a protein called Menin in older mice improved memory, balance, bone mass, and skin thickness in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing the animals with a naturally occurring amino acid improved their learning and memory in only three weeks.
The findings, originally published in March 2023 in PLOS Biology, came from researchers led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in China. Their experiments identified a previously overlooked connection between inflammation, brain chemistry, and aging throughout the body. Although the results were obtained in mice, they raised an intriguing possibility: Some effects of aging may be influenced by biological processes in the brain that scientists could eventually learn to modify.
Research published since then has added evidence that the brain plays an important role in regulating aging. It has also revealed why the seemingly simple supplement findings deserve careful interpretation.
How a Hidden Brain Protein May Influence Aging
At the center of the discovery is the hypothalamus, a small but powerful region near the base of the brain. It helps regulate essential functions such as body temperature, hunger, metabolism, sleep, and hormone production. Because these systems affect nearly every organ, changes in the hypothalamus can have consequences throughout the body.
Scientists have increasingly recognized the hypothalamus as an important player in aging. One possible reason involves neuroinflammation, the brain's inflammatory response. Although inflammation helps protect against infections and injuries, persistent inflammation can interfere with normal cellular function and contribute to age-related deterioration.
Earlier work by Leng and colleagues had identified Menin as a protein that helps restrain inflammation in the hypothalamus. Menin also participates in regulating gene activity, allowing it to influence multiple biological pathways.
The researchers wanted to understand what happens when this protective protein begins to disappear with age.
They discovered that Menin levels gradually declined in certain hypothalamic neurons as mice grew older. Interestingly, the same decrease was not observed in astrocytes or microglia, two other important types of brain cells involved in supporting neurons and managing immune responses.
To investigate whether this decline actually contributed to aging, the team developed genetically modified mice in which Menin could be selectively disabled.
The results were striking. Mice with reduced Menin activity developed greater inflammation in the hypothalamus, thinner skin, reduced bone mass, and worsening cognitive performance. Their lifespans were also modestly shortened.
Rather than simply accompanying aging, the loss of Menin appeared capable of helping drive several of its characteristic changes.
Restoring Menin Reversed Several Signs of Aging in 30 Days
The researchers then asked an even more interesting question: If declining Menin contributes to aging, could restoring the protein reverse some of the damage?
To find out, they used a gene delivery technique to increase Menin production in a specific part of the hypothalamus in older (20-month-old) mice. This region, called the ventromedial hypothalamus, helps coordinate metabolism, energy balance, and other bodily functions.
Just 30 days after treatment, the animals showed measurable improvements.
Their skin became thicker, bone mass increased, and performance improved on tests measuring learning, memory, and balance. Researchers also observed reductions in inflammation and improvements in certain metabolic changes associated with aging.
In a separate survival analysis, mice receiving the Menin treatment also lived longer than untreated controls.
These findings suggested that some biological changes associated with old age could be at least partially reversed by restoring Menin activity in a specific group of brain cells.
But the researchers also uncovered an important clue about how Menin produced these effects.
A Simple Amino Acid Offers a Surprising Clue
When Menin levels declined, the researchers noticed that concentrations of D-serine, an amino acid involved in brain signaling, also fell.
Amino acids are best known as the building blocks of proteins, but some perform other important functions. D-serine helps regulate NMDA receptors, specialized proteins on nerve cells that are essential for communication between neurons, learning, and the formation of memories.
D-serine is closely related to L-serine, an amino acid commonly found in foods such as soybeans, eggs, fish, and nuts. The two forms have different biological roles. Although D-serine is also available as a dietary supplement, consuming ordinary serine-rich foods is not equivalent to taking the form used in the experiments.
Further investigation revealed that Menin helps control the production of PHGDH, an enzyme involved in the biochemical pathway that generates serine (which was in turn regulated by Menin). When Menin activity decreased, this pathway became less active, reducing the amount of D-serine available to the brain.
Restoring Menin increased D-serine levels in the hippocampus, a region especially important for learning and memory.
This connection suggested that the cognitive effects of declining Menin might be partly explained by disruptions in D-serine signaling.
To test the idea directly, the scientists gave older mice D-serine in their drinking water for three weeks.
The supplementation improved their performance on learning and memory tests, even without directly restoring Menin.
However, there was an important distinction. While increasing Menin improved both cognitive function and physical signs of aging, D-serine supplementation primarily improved cognition. It did not restore the age-related losses in bone mass and skin thickness.
That difference suggests Menin influences aging through several biological mechanisms, with D-serine accounting for only part of its effects.
Later Research Strengthens the Link Between the Brain and Aging
Since the original 2023 discovery, additional studies have provided evidence that the hypothalamus helps coordinate aging across the body.
In a 2024 study published in Cell Metabolism, researchers at Washington University School of Medicine identified a different group of hypothalamic neurons that communicates with fat tissue. By maintaining or stimulating this communication pathway, they increased physical activity, improved age-related metabolic function, and extended lifespan in mice.
That work involved a different protein and neural circuit from Menin, but supported the broader idea that signals originating in the hypothalamus can influence how the rest of the body ages.
Another 2024 study in the Journal of Physiology and Biochemistry provided additional insight into Menin itself. Researchers found that increasing Menin helped protect cultured hippocampal cells against inflammation and a form of programmed cell death triggered by exposure to the stress hormone corticosterone. Although these laboratory experiments did not establish an anti-aging effect, they supported the idea that Menin has important protective functions in brain cells.
An even larger picture emerged in January 2025, when scientists published a detailed analysis of approximately 1.2 million mouse brain cells in Nature.
The researchers discovered that some of the brain cells most sensitive to aging were concentrated around the third ventricle, a fluid-filled cavity in the hypothalamus. Many aging cells showed reduced activity in genes involved in normal neuronal function and increased activity in genes associated with inflammation and immune responses.
These findings highlighted the hypothalamus as a potential center of vulnerability during brain aging, although they did not directly test the Menin pathway.
New Findings in 2026 Reveal More Aging Pathways
Research published in 2026 has further strengthened the connection between hypothalamic activity and longevity.
In a study published in Cell, scientists found that strengthening daily biological rhythms in a specific hypothalamic region improved several aging-related measurements and extended lifespan in male mice. The intervention also reduced estimates of biological age based on DNA methylation, chemical modifications to DNA that change with age.
Another 2026 study in Cell Metabolism identified a protein called Mimecan that helps skeletal muscles communicate with the hypothalamus and brown fat, a specialized tissue involved in generating body heat. Restoring circulating Mimecan levels in older mice improved this communication and extended lifespan.
Together, these discoveries suggest that aging involves complex communication between the brain and the rest of the body. Rather than depending on one master switch, multiple neural circuits, hormones, and metabolic signals appear to help determine how age-related changes unfold.
Could D-Serine Supplements Protect the Human Brain?
The possibility of improving memory with a relatively simple amino acid is especially appealing. However, evidence that D-serine can reverse age-related cognitive decline in humans remains limited.
A small randomized clinical trial published in 2016 tested D-serine in 50 healthy older adults. Participants performed better on one assessment of spatial learning and problem-solving after receiving the amino acid, but researchers did not find significant improvements across the other cognitive tests or mood measurements.
More importantly, later research suggests that the effects of D-serine depend on the biological circumstances.
In an April 2025 study published in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences, scientists investigated D-serine in mice genetically engineered to develop features of Alzheimer's disease.
Unlike the Menin experiments, which associated reduced D-serine with age-related memory impairment, this study found that an early increase in D-serine accompanied disruptions in brain signaling. Removing the enzyme responsible for producing D-serine prevented or reduced several later cognitive impairments in those mice.
These findings do not invalidate the earlier results. Instead, they suggest that D-serine signaling is more complicated than simply having too little or too much. Its effects may depend on the condition being studied, the timing of treatment, and how the brain's signaling systems are functioning.
There are also unanswered questions about the long-term safety of D-serine supplementation. High doses have raised kidney safety concerns in animal experiments, and research has not established whether prolonged supplementation is a safe or effective way to prevent age-related memory loss in otherwise healthy people.
For now, D-serine should be considered an experimental approach rather than a proven treatment for brain aging.
Can Scientists Eventually Slow Aging by Targeting the Brain?
Despite the encouraging mouse experiments, researchers still need to answer several fundamental questions.
Why does Menin decline in the hypothalamus as animals age? How many of its effects could be reversed by treatment, and how long would those improvements last? Could restoring Menin influence other biological systems in unexpected ways?
It is also unclear whether treatments targeting Menin or D-serine could reproduce similar results in humans.
Nevertheless, the original researchers believe the pathway deserves further investigation.
"We speculate that the decline of Menin expression in the hypothalamus with age may be one of the driving factors of aging, and Menin may be the key protein connecting the genetic, inflammatory, and metabolic factors of aging. D-serine is a potentially promising therapeutic for cognitive decline," said Leng.
Leng adds, "Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) Menin signaling diminished in aged mice, which contributes to systemic aging phenotypes and cognitive deficits. The effects of Menin on aging are mediated by neuroinflammatory changes and metabolic pathway signaling, accompanied by serine deficiency in VMH, while restoration of Menin in VMH reversed aging-related phenotypes."
The growing body of evidence points toward a potentially important shift in how scientists understand aging. Instead of viewing it only as the gradual deterioration of individual organs, researchers are investigating how specific brain pathways may actively shape the process.
The possibility that restoring those pathways could improve memory, physical function, or longevity remains experimental. But the Menin discovery, together with subsequent findings, offers a compelling reason to explore whether some of the biological changes associated with aging are more reversible than previously thought.

articles.title: NASA captures a stunning transformation in Australia's red outback
articles.text:
NASA captures a stunning transformation in Australia's red outback
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- NASA Earth Observatory
- Summary:
- Australia's normally dry, rust-colored outback has erupted into a spectacular carpet of wildflowers after unusually heavy rains, potentially producing its most impressive bloom in nearly 20 years. NASA satellite images capture the stunning transformation, which has even brought rare flowers to the grounds of a remote deep-space observatory.
- Share:
A spectacular explosion of wildflowers has transformed the normally dry, rust-colored landscape of Western Australia into a vibrant patchwork of green and colorful blooms. The remarkable display followed months of unusually wet weather, awakening seeds that had been lying dormant beneath the soil.
By late winter 2026 in the Southern Hemisphere, large stretches of the region's arid shrubland were covered in flowers. Local experts believe this could be the most impressive wildflower season the area has experienced in nearly 20 years.
NASA satellite imagery reveals just how dramatically the landscape changed in a single year.
NASA Satellite Images Reveal a Dramatic Transformation
The images above were collected by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) aboard the NASA-USGS Landsat 8 satellite. They show the same part of Western Australia in late August 2025 (left) and late August 2026 (right), highlighting the striking increase in vegetation following the unusually wet conditions.
The location is in the Murchison region, approximately 600 kilometers (370 miles) north of Perth. This remote stretch of the Australian outback is an important grazing area for sheep and cattle, with a landscape typically dominated by hardy plants adapted to limited rainfall.
Much of the region's vegetation consists of grasses, saltbush, and mulga, a slow-growing evergreen tree capable of surviving in dry conditions. Wildflowers also emerge periodically, but their abundance can vary dramatically depending on how much rain falls.
Unusually Heavy Rains Trigger a Wildflower Explosion
The exceptional display in 2026 was made possible by a series of cold fronts that carried much-needed moisture into the region.
According to Australia's Bureau of Meteorology, June brought above-average rainfall, while August was much wetter than normal. These favorable conditions allowed seeds that had remained inactive in the dry soil to germinate, producing an extraordinary variety of wildflowers across the landscape.
The colorful transformation extended into the grounds of a radio astronomy observatory operated by the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), Australia's national science agency.
Among the flowers were several threatened species, adding ecological significance to the seasonal spectacle. The observatory has helped track these vulnerable plants on land that was previously used for livestock grazing.
Where Wildflowers Bloom Beneath Deep-Space Telescopes
While the flowers created an extraordinary scene on the ground, the observatory's usual work takes place far beyond Earth's atmosphere.
Known as Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory is a remote research facility dedicated to studying the universe through radio astronomy. Its antenna arrays detect radio signals from celestial objects, allowing scientists to observe and catalog sources across the southern sky.
The observatory's isolated location is particularly important for this work. It sits within a designated "radio quiet" zone, where communication systems and electronic equipment are restricted to reduce interference with sensitive scientific instruments.
Even relatively weak signals generated by human technology can interfere with radio observations, so limiting these disturbances helps astronomers detect faint emissions traveling across space.
Australia's Radio Telescopes Have Helped NASA Explore Space
Australia's radio astronomy facilities have a long history of supporting some of NASA's most important space missions.
The Murriyang radio telescope, located in Parkes, New South Wales, helped track Mariner 2 in 1962. That spacecraft became the first successful planetary science mission, marking a major milestone in the exploration of other worlds.
The telescope also played a significant role during the Apollo 11 Moon landing in 1969, serving as an important receiving station for communications from the historic mission.
CSIRO additionally manages the Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex, one of three major facilities that make up NASA's worldwide Deep Space Network.
This global system maintains communications with spacecraft traveling throughout the solar system and beyond, while also supporting radar measurements and radio astronomy research.
Both the Murriyang telescope and the Canberra complex contributed to NASA's Artemis II mission in April 2026, continuing Australia's decades-long involvement in space exploration.
For a brief period in 2026, however, one of Australia's most remote astronomical research regions offered a remarkable spectacle much closer to home. While its telescopes continued scanning the distant universe, unusually generous winter rains brought the surrounding outback to life in a brilliant display of wildflowers.

articles.title: Scientists discover a hidden factor that can make or break chemical reactions
articles.text:
Scientists discover a hidden factor that can make or break chemical reactions
Scientists uncovered a hidden chemical variable and used it to boost reaction selectivity from 16% to 97%, potentially transforming how everyday materials are manufactured.
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- Seoul National University College of Engineering
- Summary:
- Researchers discovered a hidden factor that can determine whether chemical reactions succeed or fail, and then used it to boost the proportion of the desired product from 16% to 97%. By controlling acidity near electrodes, they developed a promising way to manufacture chemicals for plastics, medicines, and other products using oxygen and electricity instead of hazardous added oxidants.
- Share:
Scientists have identified a hidden factor that can determine whether a chemical reaction succeeds or fails. By controlling tiny changes in acidity near electrodes, researchers dramatically improved the production of valuable chemical ingredients, raising the proportion of the desired product from approximately 16% to 97%.
The breakthrough, led by Professor Jaeyune Ryu of the Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering at Seoul National University College of Engineering, could help make chemical manufacturing safer, cleaner, and more efficient. The researchers developed a method that uses oxygen and electricity to produce compounds used in plastics, medicines, adhesives, and other everyday materials without requiring the separate addition of peroxide oxidants.
Their discovery centers on a surprisingly overlooked factor called "local pH," which describes the acidity or alkalinity in the immediate surroundings of an electrode. By redesigning a chemical reactor to control the distance between electrodes and the movement of liquid through the system, the team found a way to manage these conditions and greatly improve the reaction's performance.
The work focused on two important families of chemicals: lactones and epoxides. Lactones are essential starting materials for biodegradable plastics and polyurethanes, while epoxides are used to manufacture adhesives, protective coatings, and epoxy resins found in electronic materials. Both also play important roles in producing pharmaceuticals and other specialized chemicals.
The findings were published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society (JACS), a leading chemistry journal published by the American Chemical Society (ACS).
The Hidden Chemistry That Can Make or Break a Reaction
The research builds on a technique known as organic electrosynthesis, which uses electrical energy to drive reactions that produce carbon-based chemical compounds.
This approach has attracted growing interest because it may reduce the need for some of the chemical oxidizing and reducing agents commonly used in traditional manufacturing. Such agents help reactions proceed by accepting or donating electrons, but some can be hazardous to handle and generate unwanted waste.
Until now, much of the effort to improve organic electrosynthesis has centered on familiar factors, including the electrical voltage, the materials used for electrodes, and the composition of the liquid in which reactions occur.
However, the researchers suspected that something important was being overlooked: the microscopic chemical environment directly next to each electrode.
This is where molecules exchange electrons and undergo chemical transformations. Although the surrounding solution may appear uniform, conditions within this tiny region can be dramatically different.
One particularly important factor is pH, a measure of how acidic or alkaline a substance is.
During an electrochemical reaction, hydrogen ions, also known as protons, can be produced or consumed at the electrodes. If these ions are generated or removed faster than they can move through the liquid, the pH near the electrode may become very different from the pH measured in the rest of the solution.
The researchers found that these local differences can influence several critical parts of a reaction. They can change how reactive oxygen species are produced, alter the behavior of the starting molecules, and even affect whether the finished products remain stable or begin to break down.
In other words, a reaction can fail even when the overall solution appears to have the right chemical conditions.
An Overlooked Problem May Affect Many Chemical Reactions
To determine whether this phenomenon might extend beyond their own experiments, the researchers examined more than 600 scientific papers on organic electrosynthesis published since 2010.
They found that approximately 89% of the studies involved reactions at one or more electrodes in which both electrons and protons were transferred.
This matters because the movement of protons can change local acidity. The finding suggests that overlooked pH differences near electrodes could influence a wide range of electrochemical reactions, rather than just a few specialized examples.
The team also measured how extreme these differences could become.
Even when the overall solution was essentially neutral, the researchers estimated that conditions near the cathode, the electrode where reduction occurs, could reach approximately pH 11, making the area strongly alkaline.
Meanwhile, the region around the anode, where oxidation takes place, could reach approximately pH 2.5, creating a strongly acidic environment.
These changes can have major consequences. Under such conditions, the reactive oxygen species needed to drive a reaction may become less available. Starting materials can change chemical form, and newly formed products may break down more rapidly.
Simply adjusting the acidity of the entire solution therefore may not solve the problem. What matters is the environment directly around the electrodes, where the chemistry actually happens.
Making Valuable Chemicals With Oxygen and Electricity
To demonstrate their discovery, the scientists investigated a well-established chemical process called Baeyer-Villiger oxidation.
This reaction adds an oxygen atom to a type of organic molecule known as a ketone, converting it into an ester or lactone. Lactones are ring-shaped compounds that serve as important building blocks for materials such as biodegradable plastics and polyurethanes.
Traditionally, Baeyer-Villiger oxidation often requires highly reactive oxidizing chemicals, including peroxyacids. Although effective, these substances can create difficulties involving safe handling, chemical waste, and the treatment of unwanted byproducts.
The Seoul National University team developed a different approach.
Instead of supplying these oxidants from outside the system, the researchers used electricity to activate oxygen gas at an electrode. This produced reactive oxygen species capable of transferring oxygen atoms into organic molecules.
To establish where the oxygen in the final products came from, the team conducted isotope-tracing experiments. These tests confirmed that the incorporated oxygen originated from oxygen gas rather than water.
The scientists also discovered that the two electrodes could work together in an important way.
At the cathode, oxygen reduction generates reactive oxygen species that initiate the oxygen-transfer reaction. Hydrogen peroxide formed during this process can then be converted back into reactive oxygen species at the anode.
This cooperation helps sustain the supply of reactive chemical species necessary for the reaction.
However, the entire process depends heavily on the acidity near the electrodes. If local pH becomes too extreme, the chemistry can become much less effective.
A Simple Reactor Redesign Boosts Selectivity From 16% to 97%
Once the researchers understood the importance of local pH, they investigated how to control it.
Using computer simulations and electrochemical measurements, they developed a reactor design that places the electrodes closer together while allowing the electrolyte, the electrically conductive liquid carrying the reaction ingredients, to flow between them.
The idea was to prevent extreme acidity differences from developing.
Because the area near the anode tends to become acidic while the area near the cathode becomes alkaline, bringing these regions closer together and circulating the liquid helps counterbalance their effects.
The results were striking.
Under conditions where local pH differences were not effectively controlled, approximately 16% of the relevant products formed were the desired target compound. With the improved reactor design, that selectivity rose to approximately 97%.
This increase in selectivity means the reaction became much better at producing the intended substance rather than unwanted products.
The researchers also discovered that changing the flow of the electrolyte had a powerful effect on production.
Across the flow rates they tested, the amount of product generated per unit time increased by approximately 14 times from the lowest to the highest flow rate.
Moving the electrodes closer together also made a difference. When the distance between them was reduced from 20 mm to 4 mm, the production rate increased by approximately 2.2 times.
Perhaps most revealing was what happened when the liquid was not allowed to flow.
Even though the applied voltage and the solution's composition remained unchanged, the researchers obtained almost none of the desired product.
This showed just how important the immediate chemical environment can be. The success of an electrochemical reaction depends on more than the ingredients, voltage, and electrode materials. The physical design of the reactor and the microscopic conditions it creates can be equally critical.
Applications for Biodegradable Plastics, Medicines, and Electronics
The researchers then explored whether their approach could be used to manufacture different kinds of useful chemicals.
Using their optimized conditions, they successfully synthesized lactones from 18 different ketone compounds.
One important example was ε-caprolactone, which they produced with an 82% yield.
This compound is a starting material for polycaprolactone, a biodegradable polymer used in medical applications such as surgical sutures and drug-delivery systems.
The researchers also applied their local pH control strategy to the production of epoxides, successfully obtaining products from six different alkene starting materials.
Epoxides are important ingredients in adhesives, surface coatings, and epoxy resins used in electronics. They are also valuable intermediates in the production of pharmaceuticals and fine chemicals.
Together, these experiments showed that controlling the microscopic environment around electrodes could have applications beyond a single reaction.
The findings suggest a potentially versatile way to improve the production of many commercially important chemical ingredients.
Toward Cleaner and More Sustainable Chemical Manufacturing
One of the most promising aspects of the technique is that it uses oxygen and electricity while reducing the need for externally added peroxide oxidants.
The reactions also take place at room temperature and normal atmospheric pressure, avoiding the need for separate equipment to heat or pressurize the system.
These characteristics could make certain chemical processes simpler and potentially safer.
Because electricity provides the energy needed to drive the reactions, the approach could eventually be combined with renewable energy sources to support more sustainable chemical manufacturing.
The researchers believe that pharmaceutical ingredients and other high-value specialty chemicals could be particularly promising applications.
These products often require careful control of reaction conditions and strict safety measures. Electrochemical methods may offer advantages by limiting the need to handle hazardous oxidizing agents and potentially allowing production in relatively compact equipment.
However, the technology is not yet ready for widespread industrial use. Further optimization and testing at larger production scales will be needed to determine whether the laboratory results can be reproduced economically and reliably in commercial manufacturing.
A New Way to Think About Chemical Reactions
Beyond its immediate applications, the discovery offers a different perspective on how electrochemical reactions should be designed.
Traditionally, researchers have concentrated on choosing the right starting materials, catalysts, electrode surfaces, voltages, and solution compositions.
The Seoul National University team's findings indicate that controlling the tiny environment where molecules actually react may be just as important.
This shifts attention toward "designing the environment in which molecules actually react."
Professor Jaeyune Ryu, who supervised the research, said, "This study transforms 'local pH' near the electrode from a hidden variable into a controllable design principle."
He added, "To improve the efficiency of organic electrosynthesis, we need to design not only the reaction substrates and catalysts, but also the environment in which the molecules actually react."
The researchers believe this principle could reveal opportunities to improve other electrochemical processes, particularly those involving the movement of both electrons and protons.
Rather than treating local acidity as an unavoidable side effect, future chemical reactors could be deliberately engineered to maintain conditions that favor the desired reactions.
The study's co-first authors were Seonghyeon Min and Junghoon Lee, both M.S. students in Seoul National University's Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering. Hanju Kim, an integrated M.S./Ph.D. student, participated as a co-author, with Professor Ryu overseeing the research.
Min and Lee plan to continue investigating how local reaction environments influence organic electrosynthesis, with the goal of extending the approach to a broader range of chemical reactions and manufacturing processes.
The research was supported by Seoul National University, the National Research Foundation of Korea, and the Institute for Basic Science (IBS).

articles.title: Scientists discover vanilla’s hidden healing potential
articles.text:
Scientists discover vanilla’s hidden healing potential
Researchers have uncovered surprising healing potential in vanilla, revealing that its signature flavor compound could help fight infections, reduce inflammation, and improve wound care.
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- Flinders University
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that vanillin, the compound that gives vanilla its distinctive flavor, has powerful properties that could help fight infections, reduce inflammation, and promote wound healing. The inexpensive, widely available ingredient could one day become an important component of advanced wound treatments and regenerative medicine.
- Share:
The compound responsible for vanilla's familiar sweet flavor and aroma could have an unexpected future in medicine. Scientists at Flinders University have identified properties in vanillin that could make it a promising ingredient in treatments for chronic wounds, infections, and damaged tissue.
Researchers from the university's Biomedical Nanoengineering Laboratory found that vanillin has notable antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial properties. Together, these effects could make the compound useful in developing wound care products that address several challenges associated with healing.
Vanillin is the main flavor and fragrance compound found in natural vanilla pods. It can also be manufactured synthetically using materials derived from sources such as clove oil or rice. Although best known for giving foods their distinctive vanilla flavor, the molecule has chemical properties that could make it valuable far beyond the kitchen.
How Vanilla's Chemistry Could Help Heal Wounds
Vanillin is more than just a flavoring ingredient. Its molecular structure allows it to interact with other substances in ways that could be useful for medicine, particularly in materials designed to protect wounds and deliver treatments.
For example, vanillin can function as a dynamic crosslinker, helping connect different components within a material. This ability could make it useful in creating specialized medical formulations, including materials that carry drugs or support tissue repair.
The Flinders researchers examined vanillin through a framework that connects familiar food ingredients with practical medical applications. Their work explores how the same chemical characteristics that make vanillin useful in everyday products could also contribute to biological effects that benefit human health.
"Vanillin is among the most widely used flavor compounds in the global food system, valued for its sensory attributes, chemical stability and long history of safety - and that can be transferred to other areas, such as medical uses," says Professor Krasimir Vasilev, Professor of Biomedical Nanotechnology at Flinders University and Director of Flinders' Biomedical Nanoengineering Laboratory.
A Potential New Treatment for Chronic Wounds and Ulcers
One particularly promising application involves chronic wounds and ulcers, which can be difficult to treat because of persistent inflammation, bacterial contamination, and damage caused by oxidative stress.
Oxidative stress occurs when harmful reactive molecules overwhelm the body's protective defenses, potentially damaging cells and interfering with tissue repair. A material capable of addressing oxidative stress, inflammation, and bacteria could therefore offer several advantages in wound care.
"Because vanillin's synthetic form is abundant and cost-effective, we believe vanillin-based formulations may offer safe and multifunctional solutions for ulcer treatment and targeted drug delivery, especially of hydrophobic compounds.
"Owing to its amphiphilic molecular structure, vanillin can interact with reactive oxygen species, cellular membranes, and polymeric matrices, providing a basis for its incorporation into functional formulations."
Hydrophobic compounds are substances that do not dissolve easily in water, a characteristic that can make certain medications difficult to formulate and deliver effectively. Vanillin's chemical structure may help researchers design materials that carry these compounds to where they are needed.
Although the findings highlight intriguing possibilities, vanillin-based wound treatments would still need further development and clinical testing before their effectiveness and safety in patients could be established.
From Peppermint Oil to Advanced Medical Coatings
The investigation into vanillin builds on a broader effort at Flinders University to uncover useful medical properties in everyday food ingredients.
In February 2026, the research team published related work in the journal Small, describing a medical coating developed from peppermint oil. The coating, created at the nanoscale, was designed to protect against bacterial infection, inflammation, and oxidative stress while remaining compatible with human tissue.
Because the coating can be applied to medical materials, it could provide a way to introduce several protective functions into products used in healthcare.
Surprisingly, the inspiration for this research came from a simple personal experience.
Professor Vasilev noticed that eating peppermint leaves from his drink significantly eased his sore throat. Curious about the possible biological explanation, he began investigating whether the beneficial properties of peppermint could be incorporated into a durable protective coating.
That idea led him to explore the use of plasma technology, a field he has studied for more than 20 years. Plasma processing can be used to modify material surfaces and create thin functional coatings, potentially allowing biologically active compounds to be incorporated into medical products.
The work with peppermint helped establish an approach that researchers are now extending to vanillin.
Why Vanillin Could Be Especially Useful for Future Medicine
Vanillin offers another important advantage beyond its potential biological activity: it is inexpensive and readily available.
Because synthetic vanillin can be produced in large quantities, researchers believe it could be easier to incorporate into commercially manufactured medical products than some more expensive or difficult-to-source compounds.
Its relatively simple molecular structure and compatibility with established manufacturing processes could also support consistent product quality, reliable supplies, and large-scale production.
These practical considerations are especially important when moving a promising scientific concept from the laboratory toward real medical applications.
The researchers envision vanillin eventually becoming an ingredient in advanced wound dressings, ulcer treatments, targeted drug delivery systems, and therapies designed to support tissue regeneration.
"With coordinated engagement between academia, clinicians, and industry, vanillin has the potential to progress from an underutilized bioactive to a clinically deployable component of next-generation wound care and regenerative therapeutics," says Professor Vasilev.
The findings suggest that a compound commonly associated with desserts and sweet fragrances could eventually contribute to an entirely different field: helping scientists develop better ways to protect damaged tissue and support healing.
The study, "Vanillin as a bioactive component in biomedical formulations for chronic wound healing and tissue regeneration," was conducted by Borislav Stoilov, Vi Khanh Truong, Christopher Delaney, and Krasimir Vasilev. It was published in the International Journal of Pharmaceutics.

articles.title: Just 10 minutes of daily exercise could unlock deeper sleep
articles.text:
Just 10 minutes of daily exercise could unlock deeper sleep
- Date:
- October 11, 2026
- Source:
- University of Texas at Austin
- Summary:
- Getting better sleep might be as simple as moving a little more every day. Researchers at The University of Texas at Austin found that people who exercised more frequently experienced more deep, restorative sleep, which is essential for brain recovery, memory, and emotional well-being. Surprisingly, just 10 minutes of moderate to vigorous exercise per day was associated with measurable benefits, while even light activities like walking and standing breaks were linked to better sleep and mood.
- Share:
What if getting better sleep depends not just on how much you exercise, but how often you move? Research from The University of Texas at Austin suggests that being physically active every day, even for short periods, may help people spend more time in the deep, restorative stages of sleep that support recovery, mood, and mental health.
The findings suggest that consistency could be an important but often overlooked part of the relationship between exercise and sleep. Rather than saving all their workouts for the weekend, people may benefit from making movement a regular part of their daily routines.
The study, published in the Journal of Physical Activity & Health, examined activity and sleep data collected from University of Texas students who wore Fitbit devices over several months. While previous studies have largely examined how much time people spend exercising, the researchers focused on a different question: Does the number of days someone exercises influence how well they sleep?
"We wanted to know whether it matters if someone spreads out their exercise over the week versus doing it all at once, like a 'weekend warrior,'" said Benjamin Baird, a research assistant professor of psychology in UT Austin's College of Liberal Arts. "And for sleep health, frequency does seem to matter."
Just 10 Minutes of Daily Exercise May Improve Deep Sleep
The researchers found that participants who exercised more frequently tended to experience more restorative sleep. The findings build on previous research connecting physical activity with non-REM sleep, a stage that includes the deep sleep essential for physical recovery and healthy brain function.
Chris Corral, who recently earned a master's degree in health behavior and health education from UT Austin and co-led the study, explained that deep sleep is especially important during the early hours of the night. During this period, the body carries out many of the processes that help it recover from the day's physical and mental demands.
Participants who were active more often spent more time in these valuable stages of sleep.
"That's exactly what you want," Baird said.
"Better sleep means better brain health and potentially lower risks of chronic disease and depression."
Chris Corral
One particularly encouraging finding was how little exercise appeared to be necessary. Among the young adults studied, as little as 10 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity per day was associated with better sleep.
That level of effort does not require an exhausting workout. According to the researchers, moderate to vigorous activity involves breathing harder than usual while still being able to carry on a conversation. On a scale of 1 to 10, the effort would feel like approximately a 6.
Even gentler movement appeared to offer benefits. Regular walking and taking breaks from sitting to stand were also associated with healthier sleep patterns and a more positive mood the following day.
Better Sleep Linked to Improved Mood and Energy
The potential benefits extended beyond what happened during the night. Participants who exercised more regularly also tended to feel more energetic and experience less stress the next day.
"We saw that more non-REM sleep was tied to better next-day mood and energy," Baird noted.
This connection is important because sleep affects far more than whether someone feels rested in the morning. Deep sleep helps the brain and body recover, supporting processes involved in memory, emotional regulation, and overall health.
Previous research has repeatedly linked physical activity with improved sleep, while better sleep itself is associated with greater well-being. However, many earlier investigations took place in controlled laboratories and examined relatively brief periods, sometimes measuring the effects of exercise over a single night.
The UT Austin team wanted to understand how these relationships played out under ordinary living conditions, where exercise habits, sleep schedules, and daily activities can vary considerably.
To accomplish this, the researchers used wearable fitness trackers to collect information over several months. The Fitbit data allowed them to compare participants' movement habits with their sleep patterns over time, offering a more detailed picture of how everyday activity relates to sleep quality and next-day mood.
Although the findings reveal meaningful associations, the observational approach does not establish that exercising more frequently directly causes improvements in sleep.
Why Daily Exercise May Be Better Than Weekend Workouts
The results also raise questions about how people should organize their exercise routines.
Current recommendations from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization call for approximately 150 minutes of moderate physical activity each week. However, those recommendations do not require people to distribute their activity evenly across the seven days.
For some, meeting a weekly exercise target means taking long walks or completing challenging workouts on Saturday and Sunday. Others prefer shorter sessions spread throughout the week.
The UT Austin findings suggest that the second approach may offer particular advantages for sleep, although more research is needed to determine whether daily activity is better than completing an equivalent amount of exercise on fewer days.
"Our results suggest that daily movement may be better for sleep than doing it all on the weekend," Corral said.
If further studies confirm the importance of exercise frequency, the findings could eventually influence how public health organizations advise people to stay active.
"Current guidelines don't reflect the importance of frequency for sleep health," Baird said. "Having this kind of data allows us to start thinking about whether they should."
What Better Sleep Could Mean for Brain Health
The possible implications go well beyond feeling more alert after waking up.
During sleep, the brain performs essential maintenance functions, including strengthening memories and removing waste products that accumulate during waking hours. Healthy sleep is also closely connected with emotional well-being and long-term physical health.
"Sleep is when your brain stores memories, clears waste and resets," Corral explained. "Better sleep means better brain health and potentially lower risks of chronic disease and depression."
The research is part of UT Austin's Whole Communities -- Whole Health initiative, an interdisciplinary program that works with communities to investigate factors influencing health and well-being.
The team is now preparing to examine whether the same patterns appear in a larger and more diverse population through the Whole Communities -- Whole Health five-year cohort study. This next phase will help researchers determine whether the findings extend beyond college students to people of different ages and physical activity levels.
For now, the results point toward an accessible way to potentially improve sleep: Make physical activity a regular part of everyday life.
Rather than focusing exclusively on long workouts or ambitious fitness goals, people may benefit from finding small opportunities to move throughout the day. A brief exercise session, a walk, or simply getting up regularly instead of remaining seated may all contribute to healthier routines.
"You don't need to run marathons," Corral said. "Just moving a little each day helps. Light activity counts too. Doing something is better than doing nothing."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Texas at Austin. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:

articles.title: Scientists discover why a 100-year-old mushroom disease won't go away
articles.text:
Scientists discover why a 100-year-old mushroom disease won't go away
- Date:
- October 11, 2026
- Source:
- University of Florida
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising secret behind a mushroom disease that has frustrated growers for more than a century: It involves more than 17 species of harmful bacteria, not just one. The discovery could explain why treatments have struggled to stop the disease and open the door to more effective, eco-friendly solutions.
- Share:
A disease that has troubled white button mushroom growers for more than 100 years is far more complicated than scientists previously believed. Researchers at the University of Florida have discovered that the problem involves a surprisingly diverse collection of harmful bacteria, rather than a single pathogen. The finding could help explain why the disease has been so difficult to control and lead to more effective ways to protect mushroom crops.
The discovery comes from a University of Florida study investigating bacterial blotch, a persistent disease that damages white button mushrooms and causes significant financial losses for growers.
White button mushrooms are a valuable specialty crop and a familiar ingredient in everything from salads and appetizers to everyday meals. Rich in nutrients and valued for their versatility, they are often promoted as an example of the "food is medicine" concept, which emphasizes the role of nutritious foods in supporting good health. Their nutritional benefits make them an important part of many healthy diets.
Despite their popularity, these mushrooms face a longstanding problem that can make entire portions of a harvest difficult or impossible to sell.
A Century-Old Mushroom Disease With Hidden Culprits
Bacterial blotch causes brown or yellow discoloration on mushroom surfaces, damaging their appearance and reducing their commercial value. The disease can also lower crop yields and shorten shelf life, making it a costly challenge for mushroom farms across the United States.
Adding to the difficulty, visible symptoms sometimes develop only after mushrooms have been shipped to grocery stores or purchased by consumers. This delayed appearance makes the disease especially troublesome for growers trying to ensure consistent product quality.
For many years, scientists primarily associated bacterial blotch with a single disease-causing bacterial pathogen. However, researchers at the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS) have now found that the disease involves a much more complex collection of pathogenic bacteria.
These microorganisms can thrive in the carefully controlled, humid indoor environments used for commercial mushroom cultivation. Because several bacterial species may contribute to the same disease, methods designed to target a single pathogen may not be sufficient.
"For years, the industry has struggled with treatments that provide inconsistent results against bacterial blotch," said Samuel Martins, co-author and assistant professor in the UF/IFAS Department of Plant Pathology. "As part of a separate $7 million U.S. Department of Agriculture grant involving Penn State, University of Delaware and UF/IFAS, we are developing advanced diagnostics and sustainable solutions to strengthen mushroom farms nationwide."
DNA Analysis Reveals More Than 17 Bacterial Species
To investigate what was causing the disease, the research team collected affected mushrooms from several production facilities across the southern United States.
The scientists combined DNA sequencing, chemical profiling and conventional laboratory testing to identify the bacteria associated with the damaged mushrooms. DNA sequencing allowed them to examine the genetic identities of microorganisms present in the samples, while the additional tests helped characterize the bacteria and their disease-causing potential.
The results revealed a far more diverse group of pathogens than expected.
"We found more than 17 different species of pathogenic bacteria associated with the disease," said Sameerika Mudiyanselage, the study's lead author and a doctoral student of Martins and Romina Gazis at UF/IFAS Tropical Research and Education Center. "While two well-known bacterial pathogens dominated the known disease profile, we also detected a surprisingly high level of another group of bacteria that has not previously been linked to the mushroom disease."
The discovery suggests that scientists have been overlooking important contributors to bacterial blotch. Although two established pathogens remained prominent, the presence of additional bacterial groups indicates that the disease cannot be fully understood by studying those organisms alone.
This complexity may help explain why bacterial blotch has persisted for generations despite efforts to manage it. When several different microorganisms are associated with a disease, identifying the responsible bacteria, predicting outbreaks, and developing consistently effective treatments become more challenging.
The findings also suggest that growers may need more comprehensive detection methods capable of identifying a broader range of bacterial threats.
"We hope that expanding our research will lead to the development of better diagnostics and more effective treatments to address the full group of disease-causing bacteria in white button mushrooms," she said.
Natural Treatments Could Help Protect Mushroom Farms
The University of Florida researchers are now building on their findings with a follow-up study focused on more sustainable ways to manage bacterial blotch.
One promising approach involves testing plant-based essential oils, beneficial microorganisms, and other biological products as possible alternatives to conventional chemical treatments.
Essential oils contain naturally occurring compounds produced by plants, some of which have antimicrobial properties. Beneficial microbes may also help suppress harmful bacteria or make it more difficult for disease-causing organisms to thrive.
These approaches could eventually offer mushroom growers additional tools for controlling bacterial blotch while reducing their reliance on conventional chemical treatments. However, further research is needed to determine how well the potential alternatives work under real growing conditions.
"Ultimately, our goal is to provide growers with practical, science-based solutions that help strengthen mushroom farming systems," said Martins. "By understanding the complexity of bacterial blotch and the role of microbial communities, we can develop better eco-friendly management practices that reduce losses while improving sustainability."
The research changes the understanding of a disease that has affected white button mushroom production for more than a century. Rather than being the work of a single bacterial pathogen, bacterial blotch involves a diverse group of potentially harmful microorganisms, including previously overlooked species.
By uncovering this hidden complexity, scientists hope to improve disease detection, develop more reliable treatments, and reduce the crop losses that have long burdened mushroom producers. The findings could ultimately help make mushroom farming more resilient, productive and environmentally sustainable.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Florida. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Sameerika D. Mudiyanselage, Michelle Lee, Jose C. Huguet-Tapia, Romina Gazis, Samuel J. Martins. Genomic insights into a multispecies bacterial pathogen complex driving bacterial blotch in white button mushrooms. Microbiological Research, 2026; 309: 128532 DOI: 10.1016/j.micres.2026.128532

articles.title: The hidden math of Alzheimer's could point to new treatments
articles.text:
The hidden math of Alzheimer's could point to new treatments
- Date:
- October 11, 2026
- Source:
- Mississippi State University
- Summary:
- Mathematics may hold unexpected clues to understanding Alzheimer’s disease. Scientists have developed a model showing how common metals like copper and zinc may influence the buildup of proteins associated with the disease, while also exploring possible ways to stop the process. The findings could help researchers identify promising strategies for preventing harmful plaque formation.
- Share:
Could mathematics help uncover new ways to fight Alzheimer's disease? A researcher at Mississippi State University is using mathematical models to investigate how common metals influence the buildup of proteins associated with Alzheimer's and whether potential treatments could interfere with this process.
Shantia Yarahmadian, an associate professor in Mississippi State's Department of Mathematics and Statistics, is studying how metals such as copper and zinc may affect the behavior of amyloid-beta, a protein that can clump together and form plaques linked to Alzheimer's disease.
His research, published in the journal Bulletin of Mathematical Biology, builds on his ongoing efforts to use mathematics to better understand the complex biological processes involved in Alzheimer's.
Using Mathematics To Understand Alzheimer's Disease
Mathematical modeling allows scientists to explore complicated biological interactions by representing them through equations and simulations. Researchers can then test how different factors influence a process and predict what might happen when certain conditions change.
"Every biological phenomenon occurs in the physical world -- in space and time -- and involves changes in shape, quantity and matter," said Yarahmadian, a faculty member in MSU's Department of Mathematics and Statistics. "Because of its abstract power, mathematics allows us to uncover patterns, test hypotheses and make predictions that may not be possible through observation alone. Mathematics does not replace laboratory or clinical research; it complements it by helping us understand the larger system, identify the most influential mechanisms and guide future experiments."
This approach could be particularly valuable for Alzheimer's disease, which involves numerous interacting biological processes that are difficult to study individually.
How Copper and Zinc May Influence Alzheimer's Plaques
To investigate how Alzheimer's-related plaques develop, Yarahmadian created a mathematical framework that simulates the chemical reactions involved when metals such as copper and zinc interact with amyloid-beta.
Amyloid-beta proteins can stick together in a process known as aggregation. Over time, these clusters can contribute to the formation of plaques, one of the characteristic features of Alzheimer's disease.
The model examines how metal ions, which are electrically charged forms of metals, may influence this protein buildup. It also enables researchers to explore two potential therapeutic approaches designed to interfere with aggregation.
Rather than relying entirely on laboratory experiments, scientists can use the simulations to investigate how changes in these interactions might affect plaque formation and identify promising directions for further research.
Mathematical Predictions Match Laboratory Results
A mathematical model is most useful when its predictions reflect what happens in actual experiments. To evaluate his framework, Yarahmadian and his collaborators compared its results with laboratory measurements obtained through atomic force microscopy.
This imaging technique uses an extremely fine probe to examine structures at the microscopic scale, allowing researchers to study tiny clusters of proteins and other materials.
The mathematical model successfully reproduced the patterns observed in the experiments. This agreement suggests that the framework captures important aspects of how amyloid-beta proteins aggregate under the conditions studied.
The results provide evidence that mathematical simulations can help researchers investigate the mechanisms behind protein clumping and explore ways to influence the process. Although the findings do not establish an effective Alzheimer's treatment, they offer a promising tool for guiding future laboratory studies.
For Yarahmadian, the motivation behind the research extends beyond the mathematical challenge. He hopes that a better understanding of the disease's complex biology will eventually help scientists develop more effective strategies against it.
"What drew me to Alzheimer's research is the combination of its profound human impact and its extraordinary biological complexity," he said. "My goal is to use mathematical modeling to identify important mechanisms and generate insights that may help guide future experimental and therapeutic research."

Materials provided by Mississippi State University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Shantia Yarahmadian, Yasser Alzahrani, Vaghawan Prasad Ojha. Metal-Ion-Mediated Amyloid-$$\\beta $$ Aggregation in Alzheimer’s Disease: A Mathematical Model of Chelation and Inhibitory Therapies. Bulletin of Mathematical Biology, 2026; 88 (9) DOI: 10.1007/s11538-026-01732-1
