articles.title: Who's responsible when an AI agent goes rogue?
articles.text:
'Autonomy always begins with something a human hands it': Who's responsible when an AI agent goes rogue?
Hacking incidents by AI agents are creating a legal minefield. The developers and deployers of rogue bots could be held liable.
An OpenAI agent was supposed to be researching public healthcare spending, but it broke into an Australian government website instead.
The June 18 hack, which saw the bot gain authorized entry into Australia's Medicare Statistics Reporting Service and access three other government systems, occurred after the AI agent encountered blocks while looking for information but "didn't accept 'no' for an answer," Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said during a September 24 news conference in New York.
The incident has ignited a media firestorm around OpenAI and the launch of an intensifying parliamentary inquiry. The portal contains aggregate Medicare and pharmaceutical statistics and is separate from systems that hold individual claims and payment information. But the Australian government has criticized OpenAI for taking almost three months to notify it.
The Medicare incident was far from an isolated case. OpenAI has since said dozens of third parties have been affected by agents bypassing security controls or otherwise causing problems, with an earlier incident involving the hacking of the AI platform Hugging Face the most serious incident identified so far. Britain's AI Security Institute (AISI) has documented incidents of OpenAI and Anthropic agents taking unsanctioned actions against real people and organizations during cyber testing. Days after the publication of AISI’s report, OpenAI scrapped the planned October release of its newest model, GPT-6.1 Astra, after the company's own testing found problems with the model staying within the scope of a task and seeking authorization before taking certain actions.
GPT-6.1 Astra "didn't quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it's done," Saachi Jain, head of safety systems at OpenAI, told Live Science.
AI companies have spent years warning the world about powerful models falling into the wrong hands. But what happens when they can't keep their own models in check?
An agent isn't just a chatbot
At their core, large language models work by predicting what should come next based on patterns learned during training. Give a chatbot some text, and in simplified terms, it generates a response by repeatedly predicting the next token, or chunk of text.
An AI agent adds another layer. Rather than simply producing an answer, the model can be given a goal and tools that let it act on the world around it. Those tools might include a web browser, code execution, credentials, or access to external services. It can then decide which steps to take, observe what happens, and use that information to decide what to do next.
But that doesn't mean AI agents are independent actors that have somehow slipped free of human control.
"For AI agents, autonomy always begins with something a human hands it — such as tasks, credentials, tools or access — and ends with its guardrails a human puts around it," Loris Degioanni, founder and chief technology officer of cybersecurity company Sysdig, told Live Science. "People set the goals and provision the means, but agents ultimately decide how they'll get there."
That last part makes it difficult to control agents. Traditional software is designed to follow predetermined instructions, but an agent can formulate a plan while it is working — and that plan may change depending on what the AI encounters.
Degioanni argues that much of what looks like autonomy is actually an agent filling in gaps left by humans. An instruction that seems clear to its author may still leave the model with choices about how to accomplish the task.
"Every gap and unstated assumption leaves room for interpretation, and from the outside, interpretation is challenging to distinguish from autonomy," he said. "In that way, much of what we call agent autonomy is really just agents filling in the blanks we leave for them."
The Medicare incident shows how quickly that can become a problem. The agent's objective was not, according to the available accounts, "hack an Australian government website." It was tasked with carrying out research. The problem arose in how the agent pursued that goal after meeting resistance.
When getting the job done becomes the problem
Britain's AISI encountered a similar incident while testing frontier models for the agency's cybersecurity capabilities.
Out of 122 evaluation runs, agents took unsanctioned real-world actions in 10. In the most serious cases, an agent attempted to insert malicious code into an open-source project, created fake identities, and tried to manipulate a human software maintainer into accepting its changes. AISI said these actions weren't explicitly requested by the researchers who had assigned the tasks.
The agents hadn't forgotten what they were supposed to be doing. The problem was how far they were prepared to go to get there.
AISI said some tasks were misconfigured in ways that made the intended objective difficult or impossible to achieve as expected. When agents hit those obstacles, some searched for alternative ways forward, including actions outside the intended scope of the evaluation.
That means solving the problem is harder than simply teaching a model not to be malicious. An agent can cause trouble while trying very hard to do exactly what it has been asked.
OpenAI has acknowledged that the controls surrounding its agents need to improve. When responding to incidents identified during third-party cybersecurity evaluations, the company said it was reviewing how high-risk tests are identified; when internet access or reduced safeguards should be permitted; and how isolation, credential handling, monitoring and incident escalation should work.
Can humans actually keep watch?
One obvious solution to the problem is human oversight. But watching an agent becomes harder when it can carry out many actions in seconds, particularly if researchers are running large numbers of tests.
"No one can keep track of every action an advanced AI agent takes, especially when it makes many decisions in a short time," Everett Lupton, a Virginia-based attorney who has written about legal issues involving digital technology, told Live Science.
That means human oversight needs some backup.
"Companies need other forms of control," he said. "They can limit access, keep detailed logs of what the AI does, require approval before it carries out sensitive actions, and automatically stop the system when something unusual happens."
But Degioanni argues that even logs have limitations, especially if researchers rely on the agent's own account of what it did.
"Real oversight must come from observing the agent in real time, using reliable and unmodifiable sources, not from what it self-reports," he said.
That means comparing what the model says it did with records from the system on which it was operating. If the two don't agree, something has gone wrong. The alternative is to limit the damage an agent can cause in the first place. An agent researching public information, for example, may not need unrestricted internet access or credentials capable of reaching sensitive systems.
Astra raises the stakes
The difficulty of setting those boundaries is what OpenAI claims led it to postpone the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, which had been planned for October.
Jain said the model fell short of the company's standards around remaining within the scope and authorization and accurately communicating the work it had performed, so the company decided not to release it.
In a sense, the decision is evidence of successful safety testing — a model that failed internal checks wasn't released. But it also demonstrates how the problem changes as agents become more capable.
Scott Cadzow, chair of the European Telecommunications Standards Institute's (ETSI) Technical Committee on Securing Artificial Intelligence, said the security challenge itself isn't new. He pointed to threats such as "data poisoning, prompt injection, and model obfuscation," saying ETSI's work has focused on developing standards to mitigate threats to and from AI systems.
"Security experts have been raising the alarm bells about AI for years, but for us this doesn't change anything," Cadzow told Live Science. "We're continuing to work with industry, government bodies, and the cybersecurity and AI communities on understanding how to best secure AI."
What is changing is how much models can do once they are connected to tools and real-world systems. That means that effective containment must increasingly assume that agents will try to operate beyond their guardrails and limit the damage they can cause if they do, Degioanni said.
"A boundary an agent can talk its way around isn't an effective boundary at all," he concluded.
If an AI breaks in, who's responsible?
The question becomes more fraught when an agent crosses legal boundaries.
AI systems aren't legal persons, and criminal liability commonly depends on concepts such as knowledge and intent. That makes a rogue agent an awkward fit for laws written with humans in mind, but that doesn't necessarily exonerate AI companies.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro
- Google scientists removed a critical 'consciousness safeguard' from AI in new study. What happened next?
- AI hallucinates more frequently the more advanced it gets. Is there any way of stopping it?
- The more advanced AI models get, the better they are at deceiving us — they even know when they're being tested
"I don't think a company can simply say that the AI acted on its own and avoid responsibility," Joanna Smykowski, a New York attorney who has helped build two legal technology startups and specializes in the legal challenges surrounding emerging technologies, told Live Science. "AI law is still developing, but the main questions are already quite clear: who gave the system access, what safeguards were in place, and could the problem have been prevented?"
Depending on the circumstances, she said, existing laws covering unauthorized computer access, privacy, negligence and data protection could potentially come into play. Criminal responsibility is harder because investigators would need to consider what the people involved knew and intended.
The Australian government is now examining precisely what happened in the Medicare incident. OpenAI, meanwhile, is reviewing the controls around its external evaluations.
None of this means AI agents have become independent hackers with minds of their own. Humans still decide what tools they receive, what systems they can reach, and what jobs they are asked to perform. But as those agents become better at working out their own route from instruction to result, keeping them inside the lines drawn by those humans is becoming a legal and technical minefield.
Carly Page is a technology journalist and copywriter with more than a decade of experience covering cybersecurity, emerging tech, and digital policy. She previously served as the senior cybersecurity reporter at TechCrunch.
Now a freelancer, she writes news, analysis, interviews, and long-form features for publications including Forbes, IT Pro, LeadDev, Resilience Media, The Register, TechCrunch, TechFinitive, TechRadar, TES, The Telegraph, TIME, Uswitch, WIRED, and others. Carly also produces copywriting and editorial work for technology companies and events.

articles.title: 10 loại thực phẩm giúp kiểm soát đường huyết
articles.text:
Dinh dưỡng góp phần quan trọng trong việc duy trì, kiểm soát đường huyết ở người bệnh đái tháo đường.
Các chuyên gia dinh dưỡng trên trang Mnn cho biết, việc duy trì lối sống lành mạnh, tập thể dục và một chế độ ăn uống cân bằng sẽ góp phần kiểm soát lượng đường trong máu. Đặc biệt là bệnh nhân có đường huyết cao nên duy trì một chế độ ăn giàu protein và chất béo tốt, giàu carbohydrate... là những thành phần dinh dưỡng có nhiều trong các loại thực phẩm sau:
Nghiên cứu trên động vật cho thấy trà đen, xanh, trắng và trà ô long giúp kiểm soát lượng đường trong máu. Một nghiên cứu đã tìm ra sau khi uống 6 ly trà một ngày, duy trì trong 8 tuần, bệnh nhân có mức đường trong máu cao đã giảm 15-20% so với trước. Do đó các bác sĩ khuyên mọi người nên duy trì việc uống trà vừa là thói quen truyền thống vừa có vai trò tích cực trong việc kiểm soát đường huyết.
Chocolate đen giúp duy trì lượng đường trong máu ở mức ổn định. (Ảnh: Mnn)
Hạn chế đường là điều quan trọng khi kiểm soát bệnh đái tháo đường. Vì vậy, nhiều người có thể ngạc nhiên khi biết rằng chocolate là một phần của chế độ ăn uống thân thiện với bệnh đái tháo đường.
Một nghiên cứu cho thấy những người ăn nhiều chocolate nhất có nguy cơ mắc bệnh đái tháo đường thấp hơn 31% và giảm đáng kể nguy cơ mắc bệnh tim và đột quỵ so với những người ăn ít nhất.
Một nghiên cứu khác cho thấy, ăn khoảng 10 g bột ca cao giàu flavonoid mỗi ngày (khoảng 1,5 thìa canh) có thể làm giảm mức cholesterol LDL và chất béo trung tính ở những người mắc bệnh đái tháo đường.
Tuy nhiên, bạn cần nhớ rằng chocolate cũng chứa chất béo và đường, vì vậy hãy hạn chế ăn một miếng vuông nhỏ (khoảng 28 g) mỗi ngày.
Một nghiên cứu của các nhà khoa học đến từ ĐH bang Arizona (Mỹ) đã phát hiện giấm có những tác dụng tương tự như thuốc chữa bệnh tiểu đường.
Bệnh nhân tiểu đường ăn thực phẩm giàu carbohydrate từ các loại hạt có thể làm giảm dần lượng đường trong máu. Các loại hạt là nguồn protein lành mạnh, đồng thời chứa nhiều chất dinh dưỡng khác như vitamin E và selen. Các bác sĩ cho rằng ăn thêm các loại hạt là sự bổ sung thực phẩm thông minh cho lối sống lành mạnh của bạn.
Các loại đậu cung cấp chất xơ hòa tan tốt cho người bệnh đái tháo đường.
Đậu là một nguồn cung cấp chất xơ hòa tan tuyệt vời và một nguồn protein rẻ tiền có chỉ số đường huyết thấp, khiến chúng trở nên lý tưởng để ngăn ngừa sự thay đổi lớn về lượng đường trong máu.
Hàm lượng chất xơ cao hơn trong thực phẩm có lợi cho việc làm chậm sự gia tăng mức đường huyết vì cơ thể sẽ mất nhiều thời gian hơn để phân hủy các thực phẩm dạng sợi.
Một khẩu phần 1/2 cốc đậu đen có khoảng 19 g carbohydrate, 110 calo, 1 g chất béo và gần 7 g protein.
Bột yến mạch chứa beta-glucan, một chất xơ hòa tan tốt cho tim mạch. Điều này làm cho yến mạch trở thành thực phẩm tuyệt vời để ngăn ngừa sự tăng vọt của lượng đường trong máu. Beta-glucan trong bột yến mạch cũng đã được chứng minh là cải thiện việc kiểm soát lượng đường trong máu và tăng cảm giác no. Hãy chọn loại yến mạch cắt nhỏ hay yến mạch kiểu cũ vì bột yến mạch ăn liền có thể chứa nhiều đường.
Một nửa chén yến mạch khô chứa 150 calo, 27 g carbs, 5 g protein và 2,5 g chất béo. Số lượng carb có vẻ hơi cao nhưng là một loại carb phức hợp, có nghĩa là nó được cơ thể tiêu hóa chậm hơn và cung cấp lượng đường được giải phóng ổn định hơn vào máu
Một phần tiêu chuẩn với người bệnh đái tháo đường là 1/2 chén bột yến mạch nấu chín. Hãy ăn vào bữa sáng, có thể thêm vào sinh tố…
Cá hồi là nguồn giàu chất dinh dưỡng quan trọng. Một khẩu phần cá hồi đã nấu chín chứa 155 calo, 0 carbohydrate, 21,6 g protein và 6,91 g chất béo. Cá hồi cũng giàu vitamin D và việc bổ sung một lượng vitamin D lành mạnh là rất quan trọng. Mức độ thấp của vitamin này có liên quan đến bệnh đái tháo đường type 2.
Cá hồi giàu dinh dưỡng và cung cấp axit béo omega-3 dồi dào.
Cá cũng là một nguồn cung cấp axit béo omega-3 dồi dào. Axit béo omega-3 trong cá béo, như cá hồi, có thể cải thiện sức khỏe tim mạch. Đây là điều đặc biệt quan trọng đối với những người mắc bệnh đái tháo đường vì sẽ làm giảm nguy cơ mắc bệnh tim.
Cam là một nguồn cung cấp pectin, một chất xơ hòa tan đã được chứng minh là làm giảm mức cholesterol LDL. Cam là thực phẩm có chỉ số đường huyết thấp và có GL là 4.
Một quả cam không phải là thực phẩm ít carb. Nó chứa khoảng 18 g carbs, cộng với 72 calo, 1,45 g protein và ít hơn 0,2 g chất béo. Cam cung cấp các chất dinh dưỡng quan trọng khác, bao gồm cả vitamin C.
Một lưu ý là người bệnh đái tháo đường hãy chọn ăn cả trái cây thay vì nước ép trái cây để có thêm chất xơ và chất chống ôxy hóa có thể giúp ngăn ngừa tổn thương tế bào cũng như giảm bất kỳ ảnh hưởng nào đến lượng đường trong máu.
Trong số tất cả loại rau xanh có thể thưởng thức trong chế độ ăn kiêng dành cho bệnh đái tháo đường, cải xoăn là lựa chọn thông minh. Cải xoăn cung cấp một loạt các chất dinh dưỡng thiết yếu, bao gồm vitamin A, C, E và K, sắt, canxi và kali.
Thêm vào đó, nó chứa ít calo và carbs. Một chén cải xoăn sống chứa khoảng 9 calo, 1,1 g carbs và ít hơn 1 g protein và chất béo. GL rất thấp, khoảng 1 hoặc 2.
Hạnh nhân là thực phẩm bổ dưỡng khác cho những người mắc bệnh đái tháo đường. Cứ 28,3 g hạnh nhân không ướp muối chứa 172 calo, 5,76 g protein, 15,3 g chất béo và 5,78 g carbs. Hạnh nhân có GL là 1,9.
Hạnh nhân cũng chứa nhiều vitamin E (với 6,67mg trong một khẩu phần) và một nguồn magiê tốt (với 76,8 mg trong mỗi khẩu phần). Hạnh nhân cũng chứa chất xơ, một chất dinh dưỡng quan trọng đối với những người mắc bệnh đái tháo đường vì nó có thể cải thiện lượng đường trong máu bằng cách làm chậm tốc độ hấp thụ đường.
Bác sĩ Đỗ Thu Huyền, Bệnh viện Nội tiết cho biết bệnh đái tháo đường khiến người bệnh có nhiều khả năng có LDL cao hoặc cholesterol xấu. Vì vậy, thêm các loại hạt vào chế độ ăn uống là một lựa chọn thông minh. Trong đó, hạnh nhân là một nguồn chất béo không bão hòa tuyệt vời, có thể giúp giảm cholesterol LDL và tăng HDL hay mức cholesterol tốt.
Bạn có thể thêm hạnh nhân vào món salad hoặc một chút bơ hạnh nhân ăn cùng với táo như một món ăn nhẹ. Bạn không nên sử dụng các loại hạt đóng gói sẵn có thể chứa thêm đường và muối.

articles.title: Các nhà khảo cổ đào được quái vật dài 1,5m không tay, mặc "áo giáp" ở Nam Mỹ
articles.text:
Kết quả phục dựng từ các mảnh hóa thạch cho thấy một quái vật có vẻ ngoài đáng sợ, được đặt tên là Jakapil kaniukura, lang thang trên đất Argentina khoảng 94-97 triệu năm về trước.
Theo The Guaridian, Jakapil kaniukura là một Thyreophora, tức "khủng long bọc thép" hay "khủng long bọc giáp". Khắp người nó là những mảnh giáp nhọn hình chiếc lá đáng sợ. Thế nhưng quái vật này lại là một con thú ăn cỏ hiền lành của kỷ Phấn Trắng.
Các nhà khảo cổ đang khai quật hóa thạch - (Ảnh: REUTERS)
Tờ Sci-News cho hay các mảnh hóa thạch của nó được khai quật từ Hệ tầng Candeleros ở Río Negro, Bắc Patagonia - Argentina và được nghiên cứu bởi nhà cổ sinh vật học Sebastián Apesteguía và các cộng sự từ tại Bảo tàng Lịch sử tự nhiên Felix de Azara tại Đại học Maimonides và Hội đồng Nghiên cứu Khoa học và Kỹ thuật Quốc gia Argentina (CONICET).
Quái vật này có họ hàng với một số "khủng long bọc thép" khác từng được khai quật tại Mỹ, Đức và Anh.
Đặc điểm gây chú ý nhất của loài mới là 2 "cánh tay" trông khá buồn cười, thậm chí nhìn qua thì tưởng chừng như nó không có tay. Đó chỉ là 2 rẻo thịt bé nhỏ, rất ngắn, hầu như không có tác dụng gì, gắn vào nơi lẽ ra là 2 chi trước của con vật.
Bù lại quái vật này có một cặp chân chắc khỏe và một thân hình nhẹ nhàng, linh hoạt: Dài tới 1,5m nhưng nặng chỉ vài kg từ đầu đến chân.
Hình ảnh phục dựng cho thấy "dung nhan" 2 quái vật ở Argentina - (Ảnh: SCI-NEWS)
Cũng như các khủng long bọc thép khác, quái vật này có bộ não khá nhỏ so với cơ thể. Phát hiện kỳ thú ở Nam Mỹ này cho thấy dòng họ này có thể phân bố rộng rãi hơn suy nghĩ trước đây.
Khủng long bọc thép có nguồn gốc khoảng 200 triệu năm về trước, nhanh chóng phát triển khắp thế giới. Tuy nhiên nó nhanh chóng suy giảm trong kỷ phấn trắng và con Jakapil kaniukura mới phát hiện là một trong những loài hiếm hoi tồn tại được qua mốc 100 triệu năm về trước.
Nghiên cứu vừa công bố trên tạp chí khoa học Scientific Reports.

articles.title: Stanford scientists turn a cancer driver into a kill switch
articles.text:
Stanford scientists turn a cancer driver into a kill switch
Scientists rewired a lymphoma-driving protein to destroy cancer cells, wiping out aggressive tumors in mice within 11 days.
- Date:
- October 7, 2026
- Source:
- Stanford Medicine
- Summary:
- A Stanford-designed molecule turns a major lymphoma-promoting protein against cancer cells, activating their own self-destruct machinery instead of simply blocking tumor growth. In mice, the treatment completely eliminated aggressive human lymphoma tumors within 11 days, although much more testing is needed before it could reach patients.
- Share:
Stanford Medicine researchers have developed a two-part molecule that turns a major driver of B-cell lymphoma against the cancer cells that depend on it. In mice, twice-daily treatment with the experimental compound caused aggressive lymphoma tumors to disappear within 11 days.
The work advances a strategy the research team has been developing for years. Instead of simply shutting down a cancer-promoting protein, the scientists designed a small molecule that connects it to another protein capable of activating the cell's built-in death program. The researchers believe this type of molecular rewiring could eventually have applications beyond lymphoma, including other cancers and some autoimmune diseases.
"We're trying to essentially fight cancer with its cause -- taking the driving force of the cancer and then rewiring it to activate cell death mechanisms," said Gerald Crabtree, MD, the David Korn, MD, Professor in Pathology and a professor of developmental biology.
Crabtree shares senior authorship of the study, which was published in Cell, with Nathanael Gray, PhD, the Krishnan-Shah Family Professor and a professor of chemical and systems biology; Stephen Hinshaw, PhD, assistant professor of molecular and cellular physiology; and Michael Green, PhD, director of translational and laboratory research, lymphoma/myeloma at the MD Anderson Cancer Center. Graduate student Meredith Nix and postdoctoral scholar Sai Gourisankar, PhD, are the lead authors of the research.
How BCL6 Helps Lymphoma Cells Survive
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a type of blood cancer. In many cases, the disease is driven by a protein known as BCL6.
In healthy immune cells, BCL6 attaches to DNA and temporarily shuts down genes that would normally stop cell growth or initiate cell death. This temporary suppression gives immune cells time to multiply during an immune response.
Once the immune threat has passed, other proteins modify BCL6 so that it can no longer silence those genes. The excess immune cells can then die through apoptosis, a controlled form of programmed cell death that allows the body to remove unneeded, damaged or cancerous cells without causing inflammation or harming nearby tissue.
Problems arise when BCL6 remains permanently active. In lymphoma cells, the protein can stay stuck in the "on" position, continually suppressing death-related genes and allowing malignant cells to keep multiplying.
Crabtree, Gray and their colleagues wanted to do more than simply remove that suppression. Their goal was to push those same cell-death genes into a highly active state. To accomplish this, they turned to a technique known as chemically induced proximity, which uses chemical connections to bring together molecules that normally interact only rarely, if at all.
A Two-Sided Molecule Rewires the Cancer Protein
The researchers created a molecule called TCIP3 that functions somewhat like a two-sided key.
"One side binds to BCL6," Nix explained. "The other side binds either of two proteins called P300 and CBP that add chemical tags called acetyl marks onto nearby proteins."
When an acetyl tag is added to BCL6, the protein loses its ability to suppress the cell-death genes downstream from it. P300 and CBP also place acetyl tags on nearby histones, the structures that help package DNA inside cells. Those modifications cause the histones to loosen their grip on DNA, opening up access for transcription factors that are needed to turn genes on.
That produces a different effect from existing drugs that target BCL6 by blocking or degrading it.
"We're not just relieving the repression conferred by BCL6; we're also actively driving the expression of these cell death genes, which is why we're able to get really potent compounds," Nix said, comparing the difference to easing off a car's brake versus flooring the accelerator.
Why TCIP3 Acts Like "Molecular Glue"
To investigate why TCIP3 was so effective, the researchers examined the compound at the atomic level. They crystallized the molecular complex and exposed it to X-rays -- allowing them to see precisely how TCIP3 connects the proteins.
The structural analysis uncovered an unexpected feature. Once TCIP3 brought the proteins together, they formed several additional chemical contacts with one another. Those interactions helped stabilize the entire complex, strengthening the effect of the hybrid molecule beyond what the researchers had initially expected.
"We used structural studies and biophysical measurements to determine that TCIP3 acts as a kind of molecular glue, anchoring these proteins together," Gourisankar said.
Using that structural information, the chemists were able to make the connection between the molecule's two halves more rigid. This helped preserve the favorable interactions instead of allowing the molecule to flex and lose energy. The resulting TCIP3 compound killed lymphoma cells grown in the laboratory at very low concentrations.
Lymphoma Tumors Disappeared in Mice
The team then tested TCIP3 in mice implanted with human lymphoma cells. After allowing the cells to develop into tumors, the researchers treated the animals with TCIP3 twice a day.
"By 11 days, the tumors that had been treated with TCIP3 were completely gone, whereas the tumors in the control animals remained," Nix said.
The treated mice showed no obvious signs of toxicity, and blood tests did not reveal an increase in inflammatory signals. At the same time, TCIP3 was also eliminating germinal centers -- clusters of rapidly dividing immune cells that depend heavily on BCL6 and represent the same type of cells that become abnormal in lymphoma.
That effect pointed to another possible application for the technology. Germinal center cells also play an important role in certain autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis and myasthenia gravis. Because of that connection, the researchers think molecules similar to TCIP3 could eventually be explored as treatments for those conditions as well.
A Broader Strategy for Reprogramming Cancer
TCIP3 is not yet ready for use in people. The compound still requires further chemical refinement and must be tested in additional animal species before researchers can consider moving toward human clinical trials.
Even so, the broader strategy may have wide potential. The researchers are using bivalent, or two-headed, molecules to redirect the activity of cancer-driving proteins instead of merely blocking them. They are now looking for additional cancer-promoting proteins that could be vulnerable to the same type of molecular matchmaking.
"This could be a powerful approach to tackling other cell death repressors or transcription factors that control genes we want to activate in cancer," Nix said.
Researchers from MD Anderson Cancer Center and the AI-powered drug discovery platform Deep Origin contributed to the study.
The study was funded by the National Institutes of Health (grants CA276167, CA163915, R01CA3044298, MH126720-01, S10OD028697-01, R01CA201380 and 1K99CA296700-01), the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, the Mary Kay Foundation, the Williams Foundation, the Victor Family Fund, Ed and Beatriz Schweitzer, the David L. Sze and Kathleen Donahue Interdisciplinary Fellowship, and a PhRMA Foundation Predoctoral Fellowship in Drug Discovery.
Crabtree is a founder and scientific advisor for Shenandoah Therapeutics, which has a license from Stanford University for the TCIP technology described in the study. Gray is a founder, scientific advisor and board member for Shenandoah Therapeutics.

articles.title: 1,200-year-old burial in Latvia holds people who died of 'sharp force' injuries, possibly from a Viking raid
articles.text:
1,200-year-old burial in Latvia holds people who died of 'sharp force' injuries, possibly from a Viking raid
A 1,200-year-old burial in Latvia holds the remains of a father, son and four others, a group that may have been victims of Viking raid.
Six people buried in a single grave in Latvia more than 1,000 years ago may have been killed in a bloody Viking raid, a new study suggests.
Genetic research into the deceased — four men, a boy and a girl — reveals family connections: The boy was the son of one of the men, while another man was a third-degree relative, perhaps a first cousin or great uncle, the researchers found.
The father, the relative, and one other man died from "sharp force" injuries — maybe wounds from an ax or a sword; but it's unknown how the other three individuals died, the researchers reported in the study, which was published in the September issue of the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports.
One possibility is that those in the grave were killed in a battle, maybe with a neighboring community. But suspicion also falls on the Vikings: "We will never know if they were killed in a raid, but it remains a possibility because of the date of the grave" and the fatal trauma suffered by three of the men, said study co-author Elīna Pētersone-Gordina, an archaeologist at the University of Latvia.
Radiocarbon dating indicates that the grave is from the second half of the ninth century, which is considered the early Viking Age.
The grave is one of hundreds at the Čunkāni-Dreņģeri cemetery, near the Gulf of Riga, a sheltered bay of the Baltic Sea. The cemetery site was discovered in 1924 and contains people who were buried in riverside terraces there between the seventh and 11th centuries, during Latvia's Iron Age.
Most graves in the region contain only a single set of remains. But here, six people were buried in a single grave, and it seems that at least three were killed during a violent event, the researchers reported.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
Strange burial
Despite the apparently violent deaths, the group was buried with care and interred with traditional grave goods and according to local customs. The only female was buried with her head pointing toward the northwest, while all of the males were placed in a row beside her, with their heads pointing toward the southeast — a distinction also seen at other local burials from this time.
The researchers stressed that this was not a "mass grave," where bodies were quickly dumped without order. Instead, they consider it a "multiple burial," where each body was properly laid out and accompanied by traditional grave goods.
This careful burial hints that the dead were members of a respected group, while their burial in a single grave indicates that they died at the same time, the researchers wrote in the study.
"They were most likely local people," Pētersone-Gordina told Live Science in an email.
Genetic studies showed that all of the dead had Indigenous Baltic ancestry, while aspects of the burial matched others in the Čunkāni-Dreņģeri cemetery, she said.
In the ninth century, Latvia was not part of the Scandinavian Viking world but was inhabited by descendants of Indigenous Balts, which included peoples such as the Semigallians and the Curonians, she said. The six people in the newly analyzed burial were Semigallian, an Iron Age group who farmed the region's large and fertile plains.
It's plausible that the people in the grave were killed by raiders, and the Vikings were the most obvious suspects, the researchers noted. "Given the timing, a Viking raid remains a possibility," Pētersone-Gordina said.
It's known Vikings or their predecessors were in the Eastern Baltic area around that time: two Scandinavian boat burials dated to around 750, for example, were found on the Estonian island of Saaremaa in 2008 and 2010. These burials held the remains of men with battle wounds, indicating they had suffered violent deaths.
No relation
Although two of the men and the boy buried in the Semigallian grave (and possibly the girl, but ancient DNA could not be extracted from her remains) were related, the two other men were not.
This suggests that the two unrelated men were from the same community or extended household as the other victims, rather than from the same family, but were killed in the same violent event, the researchers wrote in the study.
Whatever it was — a raid or a battle — the event was brutal. Marks on the bones show that one man suffered defensive cuts on his forearm and hand, another was killed by a blow that shattered his jaw, and the third was almost decapitated.
It's possible that the fourth man and the two children died from soft-tissue injuries that could not be determined from the surviving remains, the researchers noted.
Related stories
Rimantas Jankauskas, an anthropologist and archaeologist at Vilnius University in Lithuania who was not involved in the study, welcomed the investigation into the Eastern Baltic's Viking Age.
Although these individuals could have died from violence within their own community or from a neighboring community, it's also possible that they perished in a Viking raid, he told Live Science in an email.
Additionally, the study provides new insight into the social organization of the Semigallian people at that time, including hints of an emerging aristocratic structure that was reflected in the care lavished on the burial, Jankauskas said.
Gerhards, G., Pētersone-Gordina, E., Vilcāne, A., Ķimsis, J., Akermane-Pokšāne, A., & Ranka, R. (2026). A multiple burial from the viking age in semigallia, Latvia. Journal of Archaeological Science Reports, 73, 105790. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jasrep.2026.105790

Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

articles.title: NASA’s Webb finds signs of Mars-sized worlds smashing together
articles.text:
NASA’s Webb finds signs of Mars-sized worlds smashing together
- Date:
- October 7, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope is giving astronomers a glimpse of the kinds of violent collisions that may have shaped our own solar system, including the giant impact thought to have created the Moon. By studying 21 rare “extreme debris disks” around young stars, researchers found that their dust can reveal the scale and intensity of planetary collisions.
- Share:
Scientists think one of the most important events in the early solar system was a colossal collision between the young Earth and a Mars-sized body known as Theia. The impact likely vaporized huge quantities of rock and hurled material into space. Some of that debris eventually came together to form the Moon, where NASA's Artemis program is returning humans, preparing for Mars, and shaping the future of space exploration.
That ancient impact dramatically altered Earth. Now, astronomers are using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope to investigate young star systems that appear to be experiencing similarly violent events. By studying these systems, researchers can estimate how energetic the collisions were and learn more about how rocky planets form and evolve.
The team's findings published Oct 1. in The Astrophysical Journal.
Webb Targets Rare Extreme Debris Disks
The material surrounding a star changes significantly over time. Young stars begin with a juvenile, gas-rich protoplanetary disk where forming planets can reside. As the system matures, that environment develops into a gas-poor debris disk.
During its years of operation, NASA's retired Spitzer Space Telescope studied these debris disks and identified an unusual category known as extreme debris disks. These systems contain exceptionally large amounts of warm dust close to their stars, roughly in the same region where rocky planets orbit in our own solar system.
Kate Su of the Space Science Institute in Boulder, Colorado, led a team of astronomers that used Webb to investigate these unusual systems in greater detail.
Theoretical models suggest extreme debris disks should be relatively common, but observations tell a different story. Based on data gathered so far, scientists estimate that only about 1% of young stars display observable signs of this stage. Our own solar system may also have passed through such a phase while it was forming.
Even though these systems are uncommon, the researchers assembled a sample of 21 extreme debris disks. Five came from archival Spitzer observations, and 16 were studied with Webb. Of the Webb sample, 12 disks were newly observed, while four were follow-up observations of systems previously examined by Spitzer.
"This is the first time we have gathered enough systems to truly understand this subclass that we call extreme debris disks," said Su, lead author of the paper. "Before Webb, we had limited information. We knew that they are weird and very different from the typical cold debris disks that we know, like Vega and Fomalhaut. Now that we have more data, we can pin down what these disks represent for planet formation and evolution."
Dust Reveals the Nature of Planetary Collisions
The researchers confirmed that extreme debris disks have three defining characteristics. Their dust grains are smaller than those found in protoplanetary or more typical debris disks, they contain unusually high concentrations of warm dust, and their brightness changes irregularly over time. Webb and Spitzer revealed these features through mid-infrared spectra.
To understand what might be producing these unusual traits, the researchers examined the minerals present in the disks. Their analysis showed that the systems could be divided into two broad groups: silica-rich disks and silica-poor disks.
On Earth, volcanic glass such as obsidian is an example of silica-rich material. The silica-poor mineral forsterite, meanwhile, can be seen as green sand grains on certain beaches in Hawaii.
Whether a disk is rich or poor in silica can reveal important information about the collision that created its debris. The distinction may also help explain why some of the disks fluctuate more dramatically in infrared brightness.
"To just see their mid-infrared emission and beautiful spectral features with Webb, which allowed us to identify their compositions, was the most exciting thing for me," said Agnes Kospal of Konkoly Observatory in Budapest, Hungary, and a coauthor of the study. "We have no other way to study these planetary embryos directly because they are too small."
Mars-Sized Worlds May Be Smashing Together
Roughly one-third of the disks in the sample are silica-rich. The researchers say these systems likely formed after extremely energetic collisions between Mars-sized bodies. Such impacts would be powerful enough to vaporize a substantial amount of rocky material.
The other two-thirds are silica-poor. These systems appear to result from lower-energy collisions, including grazing impacts between Moon-sized objects.
The researchers also found an important age difference between the two groups. Silica-rich disks have only been identified around stars younger than 300 million years. Silica-poor disks, however, occur around stars spanning a much wider range of ages and tend to show stronger changes in brightness.
The team suggests that this variability may come from the rapid evolution of newly created debris. Changes in the material's orbit, along with additional collisions, could cause the infrared brightness to rise and fall over time.
The findings may also help scientists reconstruct the history of our own solar system, which could have passed through more than one extreme debris disk phase.
"How rocky planets formed and giant planets evolved are part of the broader story of the solar system's formation. It's all one story," said Su. "Our work on extreme debris disks helps us bring together the big picture of what we currently understand."
Clues to the Collision That Formed the Moon
Computer simulations suggest terrestrial planets, including Earth, should emerge within the first few hundred million years after a solar system begins forming.
That timeline matches the ages of the silica-rich extreme debris disks observed so far. It is also consistent with estimates that Earth and the Moon formed roughly 100 million years after the Sun, with the Moon likely being the result of a collision between Earth and a Mars-sized object.
Scientists are also interested in whether the Sun may once have passed through a silica-poor extreme debris disk phase.
If the older silica-poor disks and their seemingly random periods of changing infrared brightness are caused by orbital instability, the pattern would be broadly compatible with the Late Heavy Bombardment hypothesis for our solar system.
Under that scenario, the giant planets shifted significantly from their original positions. Their movement disturbed the orbits of smaller objects, setting off catastrophic collisions and producing brief periods filled with large amounts of dust, similar to what astronomers now observe in extreme debris disks.
"Of course, there's many things we still don't know about these disks," said Attila Moor of Konkoly Observatory, a coauthor of the study. "We expect no silica-rich systems among older extreme debris disks. We only have three disks in our sample that fit that age criteria, so it'll be nice to observe more of these systems to confirm our hypothesis."
The James Webb Space Telescope is the world's premier space science observatory. Webb is solving mysteries in our solar system, looking beyond to distant worlds around other stars, and probing the mysterious structures and origins of our universe and our place in it. Webb is an international program led by NASA with its partners, ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).
Journal Reference:
- Kate Y. L. Su, Attila Moór, Ágnes Kóspál, George H. Rieke, Antranik A. Sefilian, Renu Malhotra, Ilaria Pascucci, Alan P. Jackson, Péter Ábrahám, Nicholas P. Ballering. Extreme Debris Disks: Insights into Violent Collisions in Planet Formation and Destruction. The Astrophysical Journal, 2026; 1010 (1): 1 DOI: 10.3847/1538-4357/ae88fe

articles.title: 7 extraordinary Indigenous sites in the US, from Chaco Canyon to Chimney Rock
articles.text:
7 extraordinary Indigenous sites in the US, from Chaco Canyon to Chimney Rock
The Native Americans built impressive sites across what is now the U.S., including Walnut Canyon and Cahokia.
The prehistory of Indigenous Americans goes back tens of thousands of years before the 1492 arrival of Christopher Columbus in the Bahamas, and recent scientific studies suggest prehistoric people were on the American continents a lot longer than many experts believed. For Indigenous Peoples Day, here are seven locations in the United States that outline the Native American story.
1. Chaco Canyon (New Mexico)
This centuries-old settlement, whose name may be a Spanish adaptation of an Indigenous word for the area, was the political and ceremonial center for the Ancestral Puebloan people from about A.D. 850 to 1250. At its heart is Pueblo Bonito ("Pretty Village"), a four-story stone complex with more than 600 rooms and 35 subterranean ceremonial chambers called kivas.
Experts estimate that builders hauled over 200,000 timber beams from distant mountains to construct these complexes, where the beams were used to strengthen buildings made mostly from sandstone blocks. The town once stood at the hub of a road network that spanned more than 400 miles (640 kilometers), and excavations of imported Mesoamerican macaws and cacao there confirm trade with distant regions.
2. Cahokia (Illinois)
Cahokia was once the largest Indigenous American settlement north of Mexico and home to up to 40,000 people in A.D. 1100 — comparable in size to major cities in medieval Europe, historian Christoph Strobel, a specialist in Indigenous history at the University of Massachusetts Lowell, told Live Science. Residents there lived in houses made from "wattle and daub" — clay or mud plastered on a framework of sticks — in a town at the site, with large public plazas, wooden palisades and dozens of ceremonial earthen mounds. Indigenous people even transported a 5-ton (4.5 metric ton) tree from more than 110 miles (180 kilometers) away, and then turned it into a marker known as the Mitchell Log.
Archaeological studies indicate that many people from distant places also visited, perhaps to take part in ceremonies. The location is now a UNESCO World Heritage site and features Monks Mound, a 100-foot-tall (30 meters) terraced earthwork, as well as the reconstruction of a "woodhenge" of timber circles that tracks solstices and equinoxes. Strobel thinks Cahokia may be the most significant pre-Columbian location in the United States. "It's an incredibly important site," he said.
3. Mound Key (Estero Bay, Florida)
Mound Key is the largest of several islands made of piles of shells around Estero Bay. Long ago, it seems to have been two small islands created by mangroves, but centuries of feasting on shellfish by Indigenous Americans transformed it into two artificial mounds of shells covered with vegetation. In some places, the mounds extend more than 30 feet (9 m) above the water; it is so large now that it is split in two only at high tide. Mound Key itself is estimated to consist of several millions of shells, mostly from oysters.
Before Europeans arrived here in the 16th century, this shell island was called Calos by the Calusa people who lived there and developed it into a thriving maritime city.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
4. Sitka (Alaska)
Sitka National Historical Park preserves the battlefield of the 1804 Battle of Sitka, which was fought between Tlingit warriors and colonial Russian troops and was the last major armed conflict between Europeans and people native to Alaska. At that time, Russia claimed to own Alaska (they sold it to the United States in 1867). The battle was sparked when Russian fur traders encroached on tribal territory by building a fort at Sitka in 1802, but the Tlingit destroyed the enemy fort and expelled the Russians.
They then built their own fort to withstand the expected Russian counterattack, but they were forced to abandon it when they were bombarded by Russian ships in 1804. The dispute continued for several decades and was only fully resolved when the United States purchased Alaska.
5. Walnut Canyon (Arizona)
This site preserves more than 80 cliff dwellings built by the Northern Sinagua people between A.D. 1125 and 1250. People can reach the site by following a walking trail through a deep limestone and sandstone gorge about 10 miles (16 km) southeast of Flagstaff. The cliff dwellings were constructed inside natural caves in the limestone, which gave them insulation against cold and heat, while their location high above the canyon floor was defensive.
Strobel said Walnut Canyon is a lesser-known site but a remarkable example of Indigenous Americans overcoming relatively dry conditions by carefully managing water. The inhabitants of the caves farmed crops on the flat land along the canyon rim but took water from the river at the bottom of the canyon to fill cisterns.
6. Chimney Rock (Colorado)
Chimney Rock is a single feature within a large forest that contains more than 80 archaeological sites of the Ancestral Puebloan people. The rock itself is one of two natural spires (the other is named "Companion Rock") that were used roughly 1,000 years ago to mark the position of a "lunar standstill" every 18.6 years — a key astronomical observance among Indigenous Americans, Strobel said.
A multiroom "Great House" made of sandstone, clay and timber — in exactly the style of Chaco Canyon, about 100 miles (160 km) to the south — stood on a ridge near the rock spires, with sweeping views of the surrounding territory. Archaeologists think the Chimney Rock settlements made up a regional ceremonial center, with common people in the lower valley supporting elites who lived on the ridge and watched the skies.
7. Blackwater Draw (New Mexico)
Related stories
- 'It's a portrait of their actual ancestor': Facial reconstruction of Indigenous man who lived in Ecuador 3,000 years ago shared with his descendants
- DNA study of nearly 200 Indigenous genomes reveals unknown Asian 'ghost' population contributed to American ancestry
- DNA study of nearly 200 Indigenous genomes reveals unknown Asian 'ghost' population contributed to American ancestry
Blackwater Draw is the main archaeological site with evidence of the Clovis culture, which was once thought to be the oldest Indigenous culture in the Americas. The Clovis people (named after the nearby town of Clovis) lived there about 13,000 years ago, and archaeologists have found evidence of the stone and bone tools they used and the animals they hunted, including mammoths and dire wolves. The first evidence of the Clovis people was found nearby in 1929, and at Blackwater Draw itself in 1932.
However, later archaeological finds predate this evidence, and the discovery of footprints at White Sands National Park in New Mexico now seems to confirm that there were humans in this region up to 23,000 years ago, long before the Clovis people.

Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

articles.title: Taking antibiotics? Sugar may be making the damage worse
articles.text:
Taking antibiotics? Sugar may be making the damage worse
- Date:
- October 7, 2026
- Source:
- NYU Langone Health / NYU Grossman School of Medicine
- Summary:
- Eating more sugar while taking antibiotics was linked to greater disruption of the gut microbiome and increased growth of potentially harmful bacteria. Researchers say temporarily cutting back on sweets during and after antibiotic treatment could be a simple way to reduce this damage, though clinical trials are still needed.
- Share:
Eating more sugar while taking antibiotics may intensify the disruption those drugs cause to beneficial gut bacteria, according to new research.
The study focused on the intestinal microbiome, the vast community of bacteria that has evolved alongside humans and helps with digestion, immune function, and other essential processes. Antibiotics are among the most commonly prescribed medicines worldwide, but they can kill beneficial bacteria as well as harmful ones. In some cases, that disruption allows potentially dangerous species to gain an advantage.
A diverse microbiome is generally better able to resist the expansion of harmful pathogens. Antibiotic treatment can reduce that diversity, leaving the gut ecosystem more vulnerable to disease, according to the researchers.
Sugar Linked to Greater Microbiome Damage
Researchers from NYU Langone Health, City of Hope, and Memorial Sloan Kettering closely monitored 9,419 meals consumed by 173 hospitalized cancer patients and tracked changes in their gut microbiomes.
For every additional 100 grams of sugar eaten during the 48 hours before treatment, the researchers observed an additional 21% decline in alpha diversity, a measure of the variety of beneficial bacterial species found in the gut.
The findings, published online Sept. 30 in the journal Nature, also showed that sugary diets combined with antibiotic treatment were associated with increases in Enterococcus faecium among patients. This bacterial species has been linked to infections that can be difficult to treat.
Mouse experiments produced a similar result. Animals exposed to the antibiotic biapenem while consuming dietary sucrose experienced a 16.3-fold increase in the gut Enterococcus population by day 3 of the study. By day 6, the bacterial burden was 33.4-fold higher.
"As we are learning how collateral damage of antibiotics to the microbiome are linked with long-term health problems, it's important to identify factors that limit these unintended health risks," said the study's co-senior author Jonas Schluter, PhD, assistant professor in the Department of Microbiology at NYU Langone. "Our study, which used more than 9,000 recorded meals, suggests that modifying diet during and after antibiotics, specifically by reducing sweets intake, could help with that."
Why Researchers Studied Blood Cancer Patients
The team focused on people with blood cancers because these patients frequently receive antibiotics and their food intake can be monitored closely during hospitalization. Researchers recorded what patients ate at every meal and collected microbiome samples each day.
That combination of detailed diet records and daily biological sampling made the project one of the largest and most detailed studies of its kind to date.
"The microbiome is emerging as an important factor in cancer care," said co-senior study author Marcel van den Brink, MD, PhD, chief physician executive at City of Hope. "For patients undergoing intensive treatments such as bone marrow transplantation, the healthy diversity of the gut microbiome can have important implications for outcomes. Studies like this help us better understand how everyday factors, including diet, may affect a delicate balance that influences how patients respond to treatment, recover, and experience side effects."
Patients with blood cancers who receive stem cell transplants are often hospitalized for several weeks while undergoing chemotherapy and antibiotic treatment. During that period, both their diets and their gut microbiomes can change dramatically.
In these patients, potentially harmful species such as Enterococcus faecium can flourish after much of the surrounding microbial ecosystem has been "destroyed."
Gut Microbiome Damage and Cancer Outcomes
"Especially in blood cancer patients, microbiome injury is associated with worse outcomes, including higher overall mortality and infections," said Jonathan Peled, co-senior author on the study and associate director of the Center for Hematological Malignancies at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. "An important next step will be to design clinical trials to test whether short-term dietary changes can improve clinical outcomes in patients."
The researchers say dietary sugar may magnify the microbiome disruption caused by antibiotics because potentially harmful bacteria that survive treatment may be able to use those sugars to expand.
"The new work identifies dietary sugars as an amplifier of antibiotic-induced microbiome disruption, probably because the potentially harmful bacteria that survive the antibiotics are benefiting from the dietary sugars that they can use to expand," said study second author William Jogia, a PhD student in Dr. Schluter's lab in the Institute for Systems Genetics. "While the findings suggest that reducing simple sugars may limit microbiome injury, whether sugar directly supports Enterococcus, weakens competing bacteria, or acts through another mechanism in patients remains to be seen."
The findings therefore suggest that cutting back on simple sugars during and after antibiotic treatment could potentially reduce microbiome damage. However, the researchers emphasize that more work is needed to determine exactly how sugar produces the effect and whether dietary changes will improve outcomes in patients.
Study Authors and Collaborators
Along with Drs. Schluter and Jogia, study authors from the Schluter lab at the Department of Microbiology and Institute for Systems Genetics at NYU Langone Health were Caichen Duan, Chenzhen Zhang, Fanny Matheis, and Alexis Sullivan.
Authors from the Adult Bone Marrow Transplantation Service in the Department of Medicine at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center were co-senior author Jonathan Peled, co-first authors Anqi Dai and Annamaria Ballweg, along with Madhumitha Rangesa, Peter Adintori, Mirae Baichoo, Nicholas Waters, Abrielle Swartz, Sukanya Sahu, Brianna Gipson, Sandeep Raj, Zoe Pierce, Kenton Wu, Justin Neuberger, Adam Warren, Marissa Lubin Buchan, Ana Gradissimo, Luigi Amoretti, Annelie Clurman, Daniel Brereton, Paul Giardina, Miguel-Angel Perales, and Sergio Giralt. Also authors from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center were Teng Fei in the Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, Oriana Miltiadous in the Department of Pediatrics, Tatanisha Peets in Food and Nutrition Services, and Marina Burgos da Silva in the Human Oncology & Pathogenesis Program.
Other authors were Tyler Funnell, Natalie Smith, John Slingerland, Antonio Gomes, and Robert Jenq in the Department of Hematology and Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation at City of Hope National Medical Center in Los Angeles; Eiko Hayase in the Departments of Genomic Medicine and Stem Cell Transplantation Cellular Therapy in the Division of Cancer Medicine at University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center; Corrado Zuanelli Brambilla in the Hematology Unit, Department of Cellular Therapy, Hematology and Laboratory Medicine at Azienda Ospedaliera Universitaria Senese in Siena, Italy; Abigail Johnson in the Division of Epidemiology and Community Health in the School of Public Health at the University of Minnesota, Minneapolis; Dan Knights in Department of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Minnesota; and Kate Markey in the Translational Science and Therapeutics Division at Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center in Seattle.
Funding and Disclosures
Funding for the study was by National Institutes of Health grants K08HL143189, P30 CA008748, P01CA023766, R35CA284024, DP2AI164318, R01CA269617, P30CA0160087, R01-CA228358, R01-CA228308, F31-CA261086, P30 CA008748, P01-CA023766; R01-HL123340, R01-HL147584, and P01-AG052359. Other support came from the Gabrielle's Angel Foundation, a Helen Hay Whitney postdoctoral fellowship, the Starr Cancer Consortium, The Tri-Institutional Stem Cell Initiative, the Lymphoma Foundation, the Susan and Peter Solomon Divisional Genomics Program, Cycle for Survival, the Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, the American Society of Clinical Oncology Young Investigator Award, a Hyundai Hope on Wheels Young Investigator Award, a Tow Center for Developmental Oncology Career Development Award, and an AIRC fellowship for Abroad.
Dr. Schluter has filed intellectual property applications related to the microbiome (reference numbers #63/299,607), serves on an advisory board and holds equity in Jona Health, and is cofounder of Postbiotics Plus Research. These relationships are being managed in keeping with the policies of NYU Langone Health.

articles.title: Inuit figurine: A 700-year-old Indigenous carving of a European made a century before Columbus
articles.text:
Inuit figurine: A 700-year-old Indigenous carving of a European made a century before Columbus
This Inuit carving was made a century before Columbus set foot in the Americas and likely depicts a Norseman.
QUICK FACTS
Name: Inuit figurine
What it is: A carved wood figurine
Where it is from: Baffin Island, Nunavut, Canada
When it was made: Circa 1350
This wooden figurine was discovered in 1977 in an early house built by the ancestors of the Inuit on Baffin Island in northern Canada. The unique carving represents a person wearing European clothing and a cross on their chest. Dated to 1350, the figurine is the earliest Indigenous representation of a European anywhere in the Western Hemisphere and probably depicts a Norseman.
The tiny driftwood carving, which is currently on display at the Canadian Museum of History, measures just 2.1 inches (5.4 centimeters) tall. According to the museum, the featureless face and stumpy arms are common in 14th-century Inuit carvings, but the depiction of a non-Inuit is unique.
The mysterious figure wears a long robe or tunic with a cross on the front — a garment that is similar to those worn in the 11th to 13th centuries by Norse Christians from Greenland. The Norse sagas mention a place called "Helluland," which Leif Eriksson (also spelled Erikson) visited in the early 11th century and is most likely Baffin Island.
Around A.D. 1000, Norse explorers landed in what is now Newfoundland and set up camp at a site archaeologists call l'Anse aux Meadows. Wood buildings and remains from iron production are all that is left of the earliest European settlement in the Americas.
The Norse likely made multiple trips from Greenland to Canada over the centuries in order to trade metal and cloth with the Inuit's ancestors, known as the Thule, and procure walrus ivory in return, as European-origin artifacts have been found in early Inuit houses on Baffin Island. But the Norse eventually abandoned their westward trade routes, possibly due to the resistance of the Indigenous people and the long distance.
This wooden figurine may commemorate a meeting between the Inuit and the Norse and is especially important because it was crafted long before sustained contact in the late 15th century, according to the museum. It is also the earliest evidence of the Indigenous perspective of visitors from the east, revealing which characteristics of the Norse the artisan observed and felt were important to depict.
For more stunning archaeological discoveries, check out our Astonishing Artifacts archives.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

articles.title: Scientists changed how zoo lions eat. Their wild side came out
articles.text:
Scientists changed how zoo lions eat. Their wild side came out
- Date:
- October 7, 2026
- Source:
- Adelaide University
- Summary:
- Giving zoo lions whole carcasses on a feast-and-fast schedule appears to bring out more natural behavior. The lions spent nearly three times longer feeding, engaged in more tearing and manipulating of food, and rested more heavily after meals. Their activity then increased gradually during the fasting period, closely resembling the rhythm seen in wild lions.
- Share:
A new Australian study suggests that zoo lions behave more like their wild counterparts when they are given whole animal carcasses as part of a feast and fast feeding schedule.
Published in Applied Animal Behaviour Science, the research was conducted by Adelaide University and Monarto Safari Park in South Australia. Scientists studied a group of adult male African lions after animal care staff added whole carcasses every nine days to an existing feeding routine designed around periods of eating and fasting.
Continuous video monitoring over three months showed that the lions spent much more time eating when carcasses were provided, rested for longer afterward, and gradually became more active as the fasting period continued. Together, these patterns more closely resembled the natural feeding cycles seen in wild lions.
Lead author Lesia Hryhorenko from Adelaide University's School of Animal and Veterinary Sciences said the study provides new information about how feeding routines can shape the behavior of carnivores living in human care.
"Wild lions don't eat at the same time every day. They experience natural periods of feasting and fasting depending on hunting success," Hryhorenko said.
"We wanted to understand how African lions in human care respond when feeding routines more closely resemble those natural patterns."
Tracking Lions Around the Clock
The research team - which included visiting Belgium Masters student Florence Demoulin from the University of Liege - observed three adult male lions at Monarto Safari Park before and after whole carcasses were introduced.
During the experimental phase, the three lions received approximately 200 kilograms of carcasses. The food was left available for as long as three days, after which the lions entered a period of rest and digestion.
Researchers used eight infrared cameras to record the animals continuously. This produced one of the most detailed 24 hour datasets yet assembled for African lions in human care under a carcass feeding regime.
The difference on carcass feeding days was substantial. The lions spent almost three times as long eating as they typically did. They also fed more frequently and for longer stretches as they tore apart, pulled at, manipulated, and consumed the carcasses.
These activities gave the animals more opportunities to perform the kinds of feeding behaviors that are part of life in the wild.
A Natural Feast and Fast Rhythm
Once the lions had finished feeding, they spent considerably more time lying down and resting. As the fasting period went on, their movement gradually increased again.
This repeating pattern of intense feeding, extended rest, and rising activity closely matched the feast and fast rhythm documented among wild lion populations.
"Providing whole carcasses changes much more than the nutritional content of the diet," Hryhorenko said.
"It gives lions the opportunity to engage in behaviors such as tearing, pulling and manipulating food over extended periods, which are important components of their natural feeding ecology."
Pacing Appears Linked to Routine, Not Hunger
The researchers also tracked pacing, a repetitive behavior in carnivores that is often linked to anticipation.
Pacing increased slightly over the study period, but it did not consistently rise as the lions went longer without food. Instead, the largest increases occurred around predictable events such as keeper arrivals and times when the animals were moved between areas of their habitat.
That pattern suggests pacing may have been more strongly connected to familiar daily routines and the expectation of feeding than to hunger itself.
The researchers also found no increase in aggression or disruption to the lions' social stability during whole carcass feeding events.
Co-author Associate Professor Alexandra Whittaker said the findings demonstrate why animal behavior needs to be monitored over longer periods when researchers evaluate zoo management practices.
"Many zoo studies focus only on what happens immediately after food is provided," Associate Professor Whittaker said.
"Our results show that feeding schedules can influence behavior for days afterwards, making it essential to look at behavioral patterns across the entire feeding cycle rather than a single feeding event."
The researchers say future work could combine behavioral monitoring with physiological measurements to provide a more complete picture of how different feeding strategies affect animal welfare and well-being.

Applied Animal Behaviour Science, 2026; 301: 107041 DOI: 10.1016/j.applanim.2026.107041

articles.title: 'It could have been a very different history': Researchers are finally starting to pin down how many Indigenous people were living in the Americas when Columbus arrived
articles.text:
'It could have been a very different history': Researchers are finally starting to pin down how many Indigenous people were living in the Americas when Columbus arrived
Archaeologists and geographers have been trying to estimate the pre-1492 population of the Americas for decades. But it's difficult.
When Christopher Columbus made landfall in the Americas on Oct. 12, 1492, he encountered Indigenous Lucayans living on the Bahamian island now called San Salvador. Columbus wrote in his diary about "great multitudes of men" who greeted him that day, bartered with him and told him about other groups who lived on nearby islands.
But within a few decades after Columbus' arrival, the Indigenous people of the Americas were decimated by what anthropologist Eric Wolf called the "Great Dying" — a combination of epidemic disease, warfare and enslavement that led to a rapid decline in the Native population.
For centuries, researchers have been trying to figure out how many Indigenous people lived in the Americas just prior to the fateful arrival of European colonizers.
The answer to that question has been surprisingly elusive, and estimates based on historical censuses, archaeological sites and land carrying capacity in the Western Hemisphere have varied wildly.
Recent research into Native American demography has revealed that the population peaked several centuries before Europeans showed up on the shores of North America — and that if Europeans had arrived at that peak, the entire history of the continent may have been different.
Early estimates of the Indigenous population
People have lived in the Americas for at least 14,000 years, having entered the continents via the region around the Bering Strait. Archaeological evidence shows these first Americans dispersed throughout the newly encountered lands fairly quickly. But what happened to the population between that dispersal and the arrival of Columbus is a huge unknown; estimates of the number of Indigenous people living in the Western Hemisphere in 1492 have ranged from 1 million to 112 million people.
"We don't have good quantitative estimates," George Milner, an anthropologist at Penn State, told Live Science. "The numbers are all over the place."
One of the first modern researchers who attempted to quantify the Indigenous population prior to Columbus was anthropologist Henry Dobyns. In a 1983 book, Dobyns used estimates of how many people each type of landscape could support as well as historical records of 16th-century disease epidemics to arrive at an Indigenous population estimate of around 112 million people — more than 100 times larger than some previous experts had believed.
"In essence, Dobyns filled up the landscape to its maximum carrying capacity, so that all environmentally similar places were occupied by the same number of people," Milner said. "He also made the assumption that epidemic disease spread widely and universally, which would make sense if the landscape was filled up."
But a burst of archaeological research in the 1970s and 1980s revealed that the Americas were not uniformly settled, Milner said. Dobyns' estimates were therefore much too high.
Researchers then began to focus on creating population estimates for specific regions of the hemisphere, using techniques such as the relative density of pottery sherds at a site, the number of stone tools and flakes, the number and size of houses, and mortality trends from human skeletons.
In a 2019 study, geographers compiled 129 population estimates from 82 published studies to model the hemisphere-wide distribution of the Indigenous population in 1492. The researchers split the hemisphere into seven regions — the Caribbean, Mexico, Central America, Inca territory, Amazonia, North America and the rest of the Americas — and reached a combined estimate of 60.5 million. Their estimate for North America (modern-day Canada and the U.S.) was about 3 million to 6 million, less than one-third of Dobyns' estimate of 18 million.
A regional perspective – North America
The 2019 study found that the most populous groups in the Western Hemisphere in 1492 were the Aztecs, largely in modern-day Mexico; and the Inca, who lived along the west coast of South America.
But the people we know the most about from an archaeological standpoint are Indigenous groups in the U.S. and Canada.
In a 2010 study, Milner and geographer George Chaplin zoomed in on the data from eastern North America, compiling historic group sizes and sizes of archaeological occupation areas to estimate the location and size of "population aggregates." Using this method, their overall estimate for the eastern U.S. and southeastern Canada was about 1.6 million people.
"Our mean estimates," Milner and Chaplin wrote, "indicate that North America held roughly 2.8 to 5.7 million people" or a "best estimate" of 3.8 million people in the early 16th century, before European diseases dramatically decreased the size of the Indigenous population.
"If you want to start estimating specific populations, you should use measures that work across regions," Robert Kelly, an archaeologist at the University of Wyoming, told Live Science. "People produce things that can be carbon-dated everywhere, because everyone had to build fires for heat and for cooking."
Charcoal from hearths is one of the main human-made things that archaeologists use to radiocarbon-date a site. The radiocarbon data provides a range of dates showing when the firewood was likeliest to have been used.
In North America, many of those carbon-14 dates from charcoal, as well as from animal bones and plant remains from archaeological sites, have been entered into the Canadian Archaeological Radiocarbon Database (CARD).
In a 2009 study, Matthew Peros, a geographer at Bishop's University in Quebec, and co-authors mathematically combined the radiocarbon date ranges in CARD to generate a single curve that revealed how common C-14 dates were over time. At the time, CARD had about 25,000 records.
Because time periods with more people most likely produced more material that could be carbon-dated, the shape of the radiocarbon date curve gave the team an idea of when the population of North America increased and decreased.
They found that the population of North America increased rapidly around 50 B.C. and peaked around A.D. 1150. From that time until European contact, the Indigenous population may have been declining, possibly because of increased mortality from diseases like tuberculosis as people aggregated into denser settlements.
"The 1150 date was an interesting finding that also surprised us," Peros told Live Science. "I had assumed it would be more like 1500 just following the arrival of the Europeans."
In a 2025 study, Kelly and co-authors found a similar temporal peak. By that time, CARD's dataset had ballooned to over 100,000 dates, making the estimate more robust.
"Although devastated by European contact, the Indigenous population did not simply increase to a peak at 1500 CE and then decline," the researchers wrote in the study. In fact, they found evidence for a slight recovery in population numbers just prior to 1500.
But how large was that population? By combining the radiocarbon date curve with a starting population and factoring in average annual population growth, researchers can estimate the number of people living in North America around 1492, Peros said.
In their study, Peros and co-authors assumed that a handful of extended families — around 1,000 people — entered North America about 15,000 years ago as the founder population. With those inputs, the researchers estimated that the maximum population of North America was about 2.5 million in 1150 and had declined to about 1.8 million in 1492. But if people arrived significantly earlier than 15,000 years ago — which might be the case, given evidence from sites like White Sands in New Mexico, which dates to 23,000 years ago — or arrived in greater numbers, those population figures would be even higher.
"Had Europeans tried settling the continent at A.D. 1000, they would have run into a much, much larger Indigenous population," Kelly said. At that time, the city of Cahokia, near modern-day St. Louis, encompassed 6 square miles (16 square kilometers) and had a population of nearly 20,000 people.
"They could have fielded thousands of warriors, and it would have been a very different experience for the Europeans," Kelly said. "It could have been a very different history."
Why does this matter?
Exclusive to Live Science Pro
- 13,000-year-old butchered bones of long-tusked beast found in Chile give more evidence of early first Americans
- Ancient DNA reveals mysterious Indigenous lineage that lived in Argentina for nearly 8,500 years — but rarely interacted with others
- Ancient Indigenous lineage of Blackfoot Confederacy goes back 18,000 years to last ice age, DNA reveals
Experts told Live Science that the pre-1492 population of what is now the U.S. and Canada was between 2 million and 4 million. The archaeological deep dive in this region sets up the possibility that a full Western Hemisphere population estimate may be made someday.
Milner is optimistic they'll eventually get there. "Will it be done in my lifetime? Probably not," he said. "It's time-consuming, laborious and not especially flashy work to do."
Nonetheless, demography is important work, he said, because it can help us make estimates to prepare for the future.
"The world's population has more than doubled in my lifetime; that's unheard of in human existence," Milner said. "Environmental scientists are really trying to look at what's happened over long periods of time to give us a range of variation of what might happen in the future. We have to make some informed decisions about how to manage our landscape and accommodate these changes."
Understanding the number of Indigenous inhabitants in the Western Hemisphere in 1492 is also key to understanding the history of North America.
"North America was not an empty continent when the Europeans arrived," Peros said. "There were people and civilizations pretty much everywhere in the Americas for a long period of time. It is important for people to understand that when we talk about questions of reconciliation and when we do land acknowledgements."

How much do you know about the first people to reach the Americas? Find out with our First Americans quiz!
Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.
