articles.title: CMF’s first wireless speakers look like musical milk cartons
articles.text:
The CMF Speaker Series are the first portable Bluetooth speakers from the budget-focused brand that Nothing created but is in the process of spinning off into an India-based standalone subsidiary. As with many of CMF’s products, like the Headphone Pro that launched a year ago, the new speakers deliver affordability alongside unique designs and bright color options that help them stand out from the competition. While the company doesn’t directly cite a grocery store’s dairy aisle as the inspiration for its latest hardware, it’s hard not to look at these and immediately see electronic milk cartons.
CMF’s first wireless speakers look like musical milk cartons
The CMF Speaker Series are launching in two sizes with panels and knobs that can be customized with 3D printing.
There are two versions of the CMF Speaker Series available starting today in white, dark gray, orange, and turquoise color options. The $59 CMF Speaker S is the smaller of the two and features a “custom-tuned” 45mm full-range driver paired with two passive radiators to help boost the presence of low-end frequencies. The larger $109 CMF Speaker M instead features two drivers including a 10W tweeter and a dedicated 25W woofer for improved bass performance and better separation of instruments and singers.
Both speakers offer up to 18 hours of battery life, have an IP68 water and dust resistance rating, and can have their sound profile customized through the Nothing X app. That customizability extends to the design of the CMF Speaker Series, too. The multifunction knob on the front that controls volume and playback and the speaker’s entire front panel, including the vertical flap on top that can be used for hanging, can be easily removed and swapped with an alternate color or a completely different design. CMF plans to release the official design file so modders can 3D print their own unique customizations.
Other features include a dual-device connection for quickly jumping back and forth between two wireless audio sources Bluetooth 6, fast pairing using NFC, Google Fast Pair, or Microsoft Swift Pair, and audio over a USB-C cable. You can also pair two of the Speaker S or two of the Speaker M (you can’t mix and match) for a left-and-right stereo mode, or synchronize the full mix to several other speakers simultaneously, even from other companies, using an Auracast-based party mode.

articles.title: OpenAI Dot vs. Meta Muse: How do these AI agents compare? - Engadget
articles.text:
OpenAI Dot vs. Meta Muse: How do these AI agents compare?
Both agents can keep working after you leave, but they differ considerably on price, permissions and where they can work.
Meta and OpenAI now have AI agents that are meant to do more than just wait for the next prompt. Meta released Muse on September 8, followed by OpenAI's new always-on agents in ChatGPT three weeks later. Both can continue to work after you leave, run their own cloud computers and connect to outside services.
The promise is enticing: Provide an AI with a task and then stop checking on it every five minutes. Muse can go shopping, complete forms, make travel plans, send emails and monitor things such as prices. Dots can manage ongoing research, work across connected applications and perform recurring tasks, and OpenAI is closely integrating them with ChatGPT, Work and Codex.
Dots and Muse can do similar jobs, but the experience is different
Muse runs on a dedicated Secure VM with its own browser and is designed to feel a lot like messaging another person. It can be used via Muse's apps, the web or WhatsApp, and then linked with services like email and your calendar when you're ready to make it more powerful. In Engadget's hands-on, Muse turned saved Instagram and Facebook posts into organized recipe and restaurant collections.
Dot lives within ChatGPT and is powered by GPT-6 Astra. Each one has its own cloud computer, can utilize connected plugins, remembers relevant context and can keep working on scheduled or recurring jobs. Users can also grant a Dot access to their local computer to retrieve files or browse the internet, and OpenAI plans to enable users to manage multiple Dots simultaneously.
That's where the sci-fi sheen fades a bit, since these agents still need supervision. Meta states that Muse asks for permission before taking sensitive actions like sending an email or making a purchase, and OpenAI employs permissions, Custom Rules and Auto-review to manage what Dots can do, with both companies cautioning that their agents can make mistakes. Even browser access has limits: Amazon has already blocked Muse from shopping on its site.
Muse is much cheaper to try, but privacy controls matter on both
The most obvious difference is price. The free tier of Muse has a usage cap, and the Power and Maximum tiers are $20 and $100 per month, respectively. At present, individual users must pay a much higher subscription fee to use Dots, with the lowest available option being Pro 100 for $100 per month. A Business Premium seat costs $100 per user per month (billed annually) or $125 per user per month (billed monthly).
The subscription isn't the only thing, of course. The more accounts you link, the more capable the agent becomes, but that can mean access to your email, calendar, files and browser sessions (which is not something most people would give away lightly). Meta states that conversations and data within its VM aren't shared with its advertising systems, and that users can choose not to have the interactions used to enhance Meta's AI models. Engadget found the model-improvement setting enabled by default, along with a default permission option that prompts for only some actions.
OpenAI states that activity from personal-plan Dots may be used to improve its models, depending on the user's ChatGPT setting, while Business and Enterprise data is not used for training by default. Proactive Dot research is read-only until a subsequent action passes its normal permission checks.
Availability is another complication. Dots are rolling out to eligible Pro users outside the European Economic Area (EEA), Switzerland and the UK, while Dots are available to Business Premium users across supported ChatGPT regions, and Enterprise access is still in beta. OpenAI states that Dot usage won't count toward your usage limits unless the Dot is working within ChatGPT Work or Codex. Muse is currently available in the US and Canada.

articles.title: Google invests in Flo and plans women’s health wearables
articles.text:
Google has taken a stake in Flo Health, the period-tracking app, the companies said on Monday. The multi-year deal will bring women’s health data into Google’s wearables and coaching. They did not disclose the size of the investment.
From early 2027, users will be able to sync Flo with the Google Health app, Engadget reported. Fitbit readings such as sleep, heart rate and skin temperature will feed into Flo’s cycle predictions. Flo’s insights will show up in Google’s paid AI health coach, Google said.
Devices and research
The two also plan co-branded products that pair Flo’s algorithms with Google’s wearable hardware and sensors. They gave no names, prices or dates.
A joint research programme will look for early signs of perimenopause and symptom patterns linked to conditions such as PCOS and endometriosis.
“Women have waited too long for technology that understands their bodies as well as it understands their steps,” said Flo chief executive Dmitry Gurski.
Privacy promises
No data will move between the apps without users’ permission, given separately for each type of data, the companies said. Flo data will not be used for ads or sold.
That matters for Flo. In 2021, it settled with the FTC over claims it shared users’ health data with Facebook and Google despite promising privacy.
Flo says half a billion people have downloaded its app, with more than 80 million using it each month. Google launched its $100 Fitbit Air with an AI health coach earlier this year.

articles.title: I'm in Love With My Kindle Aluminum, but It’s Not Worth the Price Tag
articles.text:
Nice compact size for smaller hands or reading on the go. Aluminum back makes the e-reader heavier, but not so heavy it's uncomfortable. Colors are beautiful. Double the storage of the plastic version. Compatible with new Kindle Click remote. Aluminum is ad-free (plastic version can be ad-free if you pay extra).
TIRED
Expensive for the least amount of features in a Kindle. No warm light, and no auto-adjusting light like you'll get on the aluminum version of other Kindles. Not compatible with Kindle Page Turn Cover.
The Kindle Aluminum has no right to be this beautiful.
Amazon announced a new Kindle lineup at the start of the month, with new versions of the Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and Kindle Colorsoft. The base Kindle is the first one available, with both a plastic version and an aluminum version. It's simply named the Kindle Aluminum, while the aluminum versions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft are now the new Signature Editions with extra features (like wireless charging, an auto-adjusting front light, and a couple AI features).
The Kindle Aluminum only offers the AI features compared to the Signature Editions, while also including a different body, 32 GB of storage, and no lock screen ads. It's not really enough to validate the price change, yet still I find myself loving it.
Notably, it comes in two colors, Seaglass Green and Alpine Sky. The latter is currently sitting just a few inches away from me as I write this, glinting in the sunlight. It's the shade of blue I had hoped the MacBooks would be when Apple released its Sky Blue color in 2025, and every single reader friend I've shown it to has said they want it for the color alone. Even my editor, who strongly prefers physical books (which is hilarious given that she edits my ever-growing list of e-reader reviews, including this one), said just looking at my photos made her want one.
It's a smart move on Amazon's part. There's little reason to upgrade your Kindle if you already have one, but most generations only came in black. The last generation just had one color for the Kindle and one for the Paperwhite. Now, with the base Kindle, you have two colors of the plastic version (the classic black and Ube purple) and the aforementioned green or blue aluminum—these options could have plenty of existing Kindle owners champing at the bit to upgrade.
But it's hard to say it's worth it just for the color, since you could always buy a case instead. It's not a bad device, and there are some improvements—just not enough to justify the price tag.
New Body, Same System
The 12th-generation Kindle still has the same 6-inch screen, but the device's overall form factor has changed. The screen is flush with the rest of the body now, rather than sitting indented, and the new Kindle body is actually a quarter of an inch shorter than the 2024 Kindle's. That sounds like a small increment (and it is!), but having both devices side-by-side, it was easy to spot. The new Kindle also felt like it fit better in my palm, perhaps due to the smoother aluminum backing.
It's also heavier, thanks to the backing. Amazon says the Kindle Aluminum is 5.7 ounces, while the plastic 2026 Kindle is 4.9 ounces. (The 2024 plastic Kindle is 5.56 ounces.) Despite the tiny difference in weight between the 2024 Kindle and the new aluminum version, the aluminum felt palpably heavier to me—almost as if felt like my hand was putting more effort into holding it up. I double-checked on my kitchen scale, and it really is only a 0.2-ounce difference. I had my husband try both models, and he agreed that the aluminum felt heavier and was surprised at how small the difference really was. I think the smaller frame makes the weight sit a little differently.
Opening the 2026 Kindle Aluminum sends you to the same interface as any other Kindle. You'll have a homepage and your library page, and the same set of menus by tapping the right-hand corner dots or swiping down from the top of the page. I did find that while the page-turn speed seemed nearly identical, the new Kindle opened up books much faster than the 2024 Kindle. On the latter, I always had to wait a handful of seconds for my latest Kindle Unlimited read to open (I'll own up to it currently being Verity, my first and very likely last Colleen Hoover book), but the 2026 Kindle near-instantly opened it each time.
The other difference turned out to be the front lights. While neither model has a warm-color front light, the Kindle Aluminum's light tone seemed a touch warmer than the bright-blue tinge of the 2024 Kindle. It was still too blue to comfortably read in dark mode before bed, but side by side, I could see an improvement. It's hard to tell in my photo below, but I know I'm not hallucinating after seeing multiple similar photos already uploaded to the Kindle's Amazon reviews.
Colorful Cost
Ultimately, you don't need this Kindle if you already have one, and $190 is a steep price to pay for a model that doesn't even have a warm option for the front light. The real draw here remains the color body, and Amazon has done a good job with this. My TikTok feed is full of e-reader fans talking about the Ube shade, while the shine of the Alpine Sky is one I would've been eyeing had I not ended up reviewing it. I also like that the aluminum body really does feel like an upgrade when I hold it in my hands.
Amazon might be trying to take a page from Apple's playbook for the iPhone, encouraging you to upgrade your Kindle every two years for the new colors, the way superfans update their smartphones. While Kindle has a much lower cost of entry, that's because a smartphone comes with many more features and upgrades. The Kindle will always have one use: as an e-reader that shows you books. Unlike the second- to third-gen Kindle Scribe update, Kindle isn't providing a new homepage experience, though you will get two of the AI-powered features the Scribes have (Story So Far, to recap where you left off in a story, and Ask This Book—coming soon, to ask about a story). You aren't even getting the auto-adjusting light that aluminum versions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft will have.
It's a good gift for Christmas for someone who already has everything, or an excuse to finally upgrade your own Kindle if it's starting to lag. But you might also want to wait and see if the Paperwhite or Colorsoft Signature Editions are the way to go instead, especially since only those two models will be compatible with the new Kindle Page Turn Cover ($80) that will give you on-device page-turn buttons. Neither the 2026 Kindle Aluminum nor the plastic version will be compatible with this accessory, making it even harder to justify upgrading, but they will at least work with the Kindle Click remote ($35).
Again, this isn't a bad Kindle. The faster book openings and slightly warmer (though still not actually warm) front light, and double the storage make it a legitimate upgrade to the 2024 model. If you don't already have a Kindle, it's not a bad choice if you want to get one of the prettiest models available. It's up to you if that's worth spending almost $200 on.
You'll likely be just as happy with the plastic Ube version and spend between $20 and $40 less, depending on whether you want ads or not (though it does have half the storage of the aluminum model, at 16 GB). Still, this is a much higher price than these basic Kindles used to be available for. Hopefully we will see these Kindles on sale for Black Friday, but I wouldn't hold my breath for any good sales this year.
Nena Farrell is a writer and reviewer at WIRED. She primarily covers home and sleep products, smart home tech, gift guides, and parenting gear. She’s been a reviewer at WIRED since 2023, and before that was a smart home updates writer at The New York Times’ Wirecutter and an associate ... Read More

articles.title: The Fitbit Edge is for folks who don’t want to go totally screenless
articles.text:
The Fitbit Edge may not be Google’s best-kept fitness-tracking secret, but as of today, its existence is official.
The Fitbit Edge is for folks who don’t want to go totally screenless
A middle-of-the-road option that combines the Air’s simplicity with some of the Pixel Watch’s smarts.
The tracker sits smack-dab between the recently launched Fitbit Air and the more powerful Google Pixel Watch 5 in the company’s current wearable lineup. Basically, if you have smartwatch fatigue but don’t want to give up notifications, this is Google’s answer to the aging Fitbit Charge 6.
Much of the Edge’s specs were previously leaked, but the tracker has a 46 percent larger OLED display compared to the Charge 6, a physical side button, and is a smidge thicker at 11.5mm. It also sports a replaceable battery that gets about a week on a single charge, though that estimate drops to two days if you enable the always-on display. The tracker uses the same proprietary charger as the Air, and can also get about a day’s worth of battery in five minutes. (A full charge takes 90 minutes.) For health tracking, the Edge has an EKG sensor for atrial fibrillation detection, a skin temperature sensor, SpO2 and optical heart rate sensors, plus your typical motion tracking sensors. As for dust and water resistance, the Edge is rated IP68 and is safe for swimming up to 5ATM.
There are a few notable hardware omissions. The Edge doesn’t have a mic or speaker, so you can’t take calls from the wrist even though you can see who’s calling on the screen. Also, unlike the Charge 6, it lacks an NFC chip for contactless payments. The latter is a bit disappointing, given that the Edge essentially replaces the Charge 6 and is $20 more expensive at $179.99. That price does, however, include three months of Google Health Premium.
The new Fitbit offers improved automatic workout tracking and GPS compared to the Charge 6. The former is a revised motion model that’ll also come to the Air. Beyond supporting racket sports, it pulls in location data and routines to make inferences about activities. For example, if you go to a tennis court, it’ll assume any activity logged there is tennis. If you regularly do yoga on Tuesday mornings, it’ll infer that’s what your activity is. Google says the new model means auto activity tracking is twice as accurate and supports over 100 activities.
The Edge’s GPS tracking is also purportedly 40 percent more accurate — though it’s not using the same software-based post-processing update that Google introduced with the Pixel Watch 5. This increased accuracy mostly comes from on-device improvements to the Edge. It’ll also support turn-by-turn directions.
Feature-wise, the device is meant for people who want glanceable information, with some but not all the bells and whistles of a smartwatch. The Edge borrows much of the Pixel Watch’s design language as far as widgets and user interface go. It’s not running Wear OS, though; this is a redesigned Fitbit OS. It’ll also get the same Google Health software updates for features like blood pressure trends and insulin resistance levels. As far as non-fitness tracking features go, it has a clock, timers, alarms, media controls, and push notifications. It also supports heart rate broadcasting to certain gym equipment.
Despite the screen, the overall look is more in line with the Air. The Edge will launch with several types of straps so you can adjust the style to fit various occasions, including metal links to give it more of a jewelry-like feel. (Speaking of jewelry-like styling, the Air is also getting a new metal mesh strap that costs $69.99 and is available October 27th.) As with the Air and Pixel Watch 5, there’ll be a Stephen Curry edition of the Edge that will cost $219.99.

articles.title: How Red Bull's F1 team is using AI to make split-second decisions for Max Verstappen
articles.text:
Red Bull Racing is now using artificial intelligence to help team staff make critical race-day decisions.
Across Formula 1, tech giants are expanding their partnerships with racing teams as AI finds its way into everything from race strategy to fan engagement. Google is working with McLaren to integrate its Gemini AI tools, while Mercedes-AMG Petronas has partnered with Microsoft to use AI and cloud technology for performance analysis and race strategy. Ferrari, meanwhile, is working with IBM to develop AI-powered experiences for fans.
Red Bull Racing and Oracle have developed an AI-powered strategy agent to help engineers interpret Formula 1 regulations and past rulings. Initially designed as a search tool, the system has evolved to recommend actions during races, Jack Harington, head of technical and performance partnerships at Oracle Red Bull Racing, told CNBC in an interview.
Initially a search tool, the system has evolved into an agentic AI that draws on a wider range of information sources, Harington said.
"It's actually making decisions for us," he added.
As an example, Harington pointed to the 2025 Italian Grand Prix in Monza, when Max Verstappen cut a corner while defending his position. The AI agent recommended that Red Bull give back the position to avoid a potential penalty, he added.
While that went against the team's competitive instincts, Red Bull followed the advice, and Verstappen subsequently overtook his rival, Harington said.
Still, Harington stressed that humans remain involved in the decision-making process.
"Formula One is and will always be a human sport," he said. He does not see AI completely replacing engineers and strategists, but rather enhancing their capabilities and allowing them to focus on their strengths, noting that there are "so many different variables" in Formula 1, from what happens on and off the track to the broader championship picture.
The team also had reason to celebrate on the track Sunday, as Max Verstappen claimed his first-ever Singapore Grand Prix victory, taking his career win tally to 73.

articles.title: Six Flags shares plunge after-hours following report of deadly roller coaster incident
articles.text:
Shares of Six Flags Entertainment plunged more than 10% in after-hours trading Monday following reports of a deadly roller coaster incident at one of its amusement parks in Georgia, marking a sharp reversal from gains during the regular session.
The stock had closed 4.5% higher during regular trading before the after-hours sell-off.
One person died and several others were injured in an incident involving the park's 200-foot-tall Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia in Cobb County shortly before 4 p.m. Monday, according to the report, citing local police.
Police did not provide additional details about the incident, the report showed.
Witnesses told a local news station they saw a man fall from the roller coaster and strike the ride several times. Riders were later seen being evacuated from the roller coaster after it stopped near the top of the ride, the report said.
Six Flags said its park staff and local authorities responded immediately to the incident, adding that it was cooperating fully with the investigation, had temporarily closed similar attractions across its parks and would not release further details out of respect for the family's privacy, according to the report.
The company's shares have fallen 22% year to date.

articles.title: CCTV Script 13/10/26
articles.text:
– This is the script of CNBC's financial news report for China's CCTV on October 13 2026.
Elevated French sovereign bond yields are expanding their impact from fixed income markets into government budget planning.
Data indicates that France's public debt has now approached 3.6 trillion euros, or roughly 120% of gross domestic product. Accumulating debt loads and persistent high interest rates continue to push debt servicing costs, specifically interest expenses, higher, further squeezing the government's fiscal headroom. A recent study commissioned by the French Ministry of Economy and Finance shows that debt servicing costs have become one of the most burdensome items in the national budget, with spending projected to rise 59% by 2030 and potentially surpass defense expenditures.
Beyond elevated yield levels, the widening spread between French and German benchmark sovereign bonds reflects growing investor unease over France's fiscal trajectory and debt servicing capacity.
Against this backdrop, a rare yield inversion has emerged between select corporate bonds and French sovereign debt. In effect, market participants perceive the default risk of these corporations as lower than the credit risk of the French state.
Bloomberg compiled data shows that as of October 7th, 38% of high grade French corporate bonds were trading at yields below equivalent maturity government debt. The volume of affected corporate debt reached nearly 215 billion euros, up sharply from just 12 billion euros at the start of the year.
KEVIN THOZET
Portfolio Advisor and Member of the Investment Committee
Carmignac
"The very poor visibility we can have on future, let's say, fiscal policies. Given again very fragmented opinions, well, investors are keener to invest in, let's say, companies where you do have much more of a strategic view. So I'd say that that would be one. Clearly, I think that this is something to continue."
More concerningly, selling pressure in French sovereign debt has spilled over into other Eurozone member states, stoking market fears that further contagion could plunge Europe back into a sovereign debt crisis.
During the first week of this month, the spread between 10 year Italian government bonds and equivalent German Bunds approached 130 basis points, marking its largest weekly expansion since the pandemic.
In response to disorderly yield fragmentation among member states, the European Central Bank could consider deploying its Transmission Protection Instrument to purchase sovereign bonds in secondary markets and contain borrowing costs. However, because France remains subject to the European Union's Excessive Deficit Procedure and lacks a politically credible fiscal consolidation plan, the ECB faces a policy dilemma between preventing systemic crisis contagion and avoiding the appearance of monetizing fiscal deficits.
JEAN CLAUDE TRICHET
Former President
ECB
"The main problem for them was to be credible in terms of budget and budget negotiation and prove that they can deliver something which would be credible. You don't win in a situation of that kind, which incorporates an element of speculation, without the country itself convincing the market participants that it goes in the right direction."

articles.title: SK Hynix, SoftBank shares plunge as tech stocks in Asia track Wall Street chip sell-off
articles.text:
Asian technology stocks fell Tuesday as a sell-off in U.S. semiconductor shares spilled into regional markets, with worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition denting sentiment.
Shares of South Korean chip giant SK Hynix, a leading supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips used in artificial intelligence applications, plunged more than 8%, while rival Samsung Electronics shed 6.7% — both hit their lowest levels since August.
In Japan, shares of tech-focused investment giant SoftBank Group sank 8.8%. The group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry, led a broader retreat in Japanese semiconductor and electronics shares.
Tokyo Electron, a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, dropped 6.75%, while Advantest, which makes semiconductor testing equipment, declined 5.65%. Other Japanese technology stocks also came under pressure. Lasertec fell 4.94%, Disco lost 4.69% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.64%.
The declines followed a weak session for technology stocks on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.44% on Monday. U.S. memory chipmaker Micron Technology slid 3.9% as investors assessed intensifying competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, which reported progress on a new chip structure.
The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the artificial intelligence boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply.
Investors are also looking ahead to a busy week of corporate earnings and U.S. inflation data, which could provide fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates.

articles.title: Global economy to slow less than expected in 2026 as AI boom offsets war hit: IMF
articles.text:
BANGKOK — The International Monetary Fund has raised its forecast for global economic growth this year as the AI-driven investment boom helps offset some of the impact from surging energy costs.
The IMF expects the global economy to grow at 3.1% in 2026, up from the 3% projected in July, but slower than the 3.5% rate last year. For 2027, it kept the forecast unchanged at 3.4%.
The UN agency expects inflation at 4.1% in 2027, above the 3.9% it projected in July – when it estimated the Strait of Hormuz would reopen by mid-July, with conditions broadly returning to pre-war levels by March 2027. For the current year, it maintained its 4.7% outlook.
The IMF now estimates that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March next year and return to pre-war state by October. Gulf crude exports averaged 88% of pre-conflict levels in September as traffic picked up, the international body said.
The report was released at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok this week, where finance ministers and central bank governors from the fund's 191 members are meeting to discuss geopolitical tensions, mounting public debt and artificial intelligence.
AI-related investment gave the global economy a "demand impulse" that helped activity in the first half of the year hold up better than expected, despite the Middle East war and trade tensions, the IMF said. Financial markets also stayed largely calm, which the fund said may partly reflect "AI-related exuberance."
For now, "use of buffers and adaptability have helped economies weather the negative shocks," the IMF said, citing measures such as diversifying fuel sources, tapping strategic reserves that have contained the energy-market turmoil unleashed by the Middle East war.
But that cushion is "rapidly narrowing" in the near term, it said. Global oil reserves are being drawn down by about 2.7 million barrels a day, nearing levels that could trigger sharp price moves, and energy constraints could impair the AI-led momentum. The growing unease over governments' fiscal health also adds to the headwinds.
Skewed growth
Overall growth is also becoming increasingly uneven. Thirty-two economies now account for 95% of global growth, down from 54 in April.
Countries that have limited exposure to the war-led supply shock and are catering to the AI-led demand are holding up or strengthening. Taiwan is forecast to grow 10.7% this year and South Korea 3.3%, up from 1.1% in 2025 on semiconductor demand. The U.S. is projected to expand 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, supported by private consumption, fiscal policy and tech investment.
Energy importers outside that tech supply chain face higher import bills, weaker real incomes and less fiscal room. The euro zone is estimated to eke out just 1.1% growth this year amid higher energy costs and weak consumer confidence. The Middle East and Central Asia is projected to contract 0.3% this year, with Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar facing double-digit declines before double-digit rebounds in 2027.
China is forecast to grow 4.5% this year and 4.0% in 2027, with higher oil prices and structural headwinds weighing on activity. Second-quarter growth of 4.3% was weaker than expected as sluggish consumption and property strains outweighed robust exports.
"The global economy is not simply slowing or accelerating; rather, growth is being reallocated across countries according to their exposure to the war-induced supply shock and AI-related demand strength," the IMF said.
AI-related risks
While AI has underpinned resilience, the investment boom is also adding to inflationary pressures and financial fragility, the IMF said.
"This is a large, front-loaded demand shock" that sees massive investment pouring into sectors such as semiconductors, data centers, and power generation, before any broad productivity gains have materialized, it said in the report.
A potential reassessment of AI-related profitability and productivity prospects could see excessive investment pull back and force a sharp correction in equities. The IMF warned that in a scenario where AI productivity gains fail to materialize, U.S. equities could fall 20% and global growth could end up 1.1% below its baseline estimates by 2028, with Asia 1.7% lower.
Fiscal constraints
Advanced-economy benchmark yields have climbed to multidecade highs as resurgent inflation, the expected path of policy rates and fiscal concerns push up borrowing costs, the IMF said. Technology firms borrowing to finance AI investment are adding to the pressure.
Public debt in advanced economies is projected to reach 115% of GDP by 2031, from 108% in 2025. In emerging and developing economies, it is forecast to climb to 84% from 74%. Primary deficits in the largest economies remain substantially larger than before the pandemic, and governments face higher real interest rates and shorter debt maturities as defense spending pressures mount.
Rebuilding fiscal space is "increasingly urgent," it said, urging governments to keep support for households facing higher energy and food costs "temporary, targeted, and nondistortionary."
Its models put the probability that global inflation exceeds 5% in 2027 at about 35%, up from 30% in April. Risks remain "tilted to the downside," the fund said.

articles.title: CNBC Daily Open: Trump defends diesel deal
articles.text:
Hello, this is Hui Jie writing to you from Singapore. Welcome to another edition of CNBC's Daily Open.
Ceasefires normally require both sides to agree to stop the fighting. But U.S. President Donald Trump appears to have streamlined the process: Just tell them they have.
"Well, they agreed. You know why? Because I said, 'You agree.' That's why," Trump said when asked why Russia and Ukraine denied accepting his proposed energy ceasefire.
According to Kyiv, Russian drones did not get the memo. Ukraine says six of its energy facilities were attacked Monday, while analysts doubt Trump's separate deal to bring Russian diesel onto the market will provide much relief at American pumps.
What you need to know today
U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday defended his decision to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian diesel, despite bipartisan criticism that the agreement could help finance Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
“I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
This comes as seven senators — four Republicans and three Democrats — have called on the administration to reverse course, arguing that Washington "should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians."
Trump argues that the additional supply will help lower record diesel prices ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Analysts are less convinced, saying the initial shipments are modest relative to the global market, while damaged Russian refineries and logistical hurdles raise questions about how quickly the fuel can arrive.
The easing of Russian sanctions comes alongside a confused energy ceasefire that Trump had purportedly brokered between Kyiv and Moscow. 
Overnight, fresh Russian drone attacks hit Ukraine, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accusing Moscow of breaking the ceasefire and warning that his country will retaliate.
"It is increasingly evident that Russia is unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire proposed by the United States and intends to continue its terrorist air attacks against our people and communities," Zelenskyy said Monday in a post on X. "Today alone, the Russians have attacked 6 energy facilities in Ukraine."
Oil markets were also hardly reassured by Trump's claims of a ceasefire and any prospects of increased diesel supply. Brent crude futures added 1.8% to close at $106.65 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures gained 2% to settle at $93.74 on Monday.
The uncertainty was heightened further as Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen attacked King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh on Saturday, leaving 12 people dead and more than 300 injured in a major escalation.
Higher prices, higher rates
All the developments in the energy markets also means that high energy prices are likely to continue to pose an inflation headache to the U.S. Federal Reserve.
Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack warned that higher interest rates may be necessary to prevent an “inflationary mindset” from becoming entrenched among businesses and consumers.
Hammack said the Fed should move relatively quickly toward a restrictive policy stance, favoring smaller and more frequent adjustments over waiting until a larger correction becomes necessary.
Markets expectations are pricing in one more Fed hike before the year is out, with traders expecting a 79.5% chance of a rate hike in the meeting starting Oct. 28, according to the CME Fedwatch tool.
Over in the tech world, Microsoft will ramp up use of its homegrown artificial intelligence chips after previously mainly relying on Nvidia's graphics processing units.
Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests.
Nvidia's GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and are found in data centers owned by companies like OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft themselves.
IMF in Bangkok
Over in Thailand, the International Monetary Fund's Annual Meetings in Bangkok are entering its second day.
The IMF is expected to release its latest economic outlook forecast, what would offer some clues on how the fund sees the road ahead. Investors will also watch for whether it holds its global growth forecast near 3%, and how loudly it flags inflation risks. 
Then on Friday comes the most closely watched event: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh in conversation with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva. It's his last scheduled public appearance before the Fed meets October 27 and 28.
— Lim Hui Jie, Anniek Bao
And finally...
Elon Musk gives $276 million to Republican groups, becomes biggest known 2026 midterm donor
Elon Musk spent more than $276 million in newly disclosed donations to Republican groups since July, making him the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterm election as the party fights to hold its majorities in Washington this November.
The largest share – $158 million – went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing Republican Senate candidates, according to figures provided by Musk's representatives to The New York Times and confirmed Monday to CNBC by Lindsey Curnutte, a spokesperson for Musk's America PAC.
The new contributions bring Musk's known federal political giving for the 2025-26 cycle to roughly $366 million, already surpassing the approximately $290 million he spent during the 2024 presidential election.
— Luke Fountain

articles.title: 'Boring is not bad': CEO of Southeast Asia's largest bank pitches Singapore as a haven amid global turmoil
articles.text:
SINGAPORE — Southeast Asia's biggest bank by assets is making a pitch to investors that Singapore and its businesses can help them navigate many of the uncertainties around the globe.
"I love it that the 'Little Red Dot' we all call home was open … predictable, and almost kind of boring," said CEO of DBS Group Tan Su Shan at the DBS Asia Future Forward conference in Singapore, referring to the city-state by one of its nicknames. "In this huge time of volatility, 'boring' is not bad, right?"
The investing and business climate worldwide has been upended by everything from trade wars and El Niño-related weather issues to the Iran conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war. Singapore, with its AAA-rated debt, stable political environment and position at the heart of Asia, is seen by many as a bastion of stability.
Tan said similar characteristics define DBS.
DBS has "one of the safest credit ratings in the world," she told CNBC in an interview on the sidelines of the conference. Temasek, the state-owned global investment company that managed assets worth 518 billion Singapore dollars ($404 billion) as of March 31 and is seen as contributing to Singapore's fiscal stability, is DBS's biggest shareholder.
DBS is also in a strong position to navigate the economic uncertainty around the world, Tan said.
"Trade and supply chains are all fragmented," she said. "If you need to diversify your upstream supply chain, just because you're worried about geopolitics, because you're worried about blockages, because you're worried about the war and the Strait of Hormuz, DBS is a partner to help you ... We can help our customers pivot from one market to another quite quickly."
Tan also addressed management of a workforce in the age of artificial intelligence, and how to find people who have the right skills to navigate the technology.
"Humans intrinsically are nimble and agile ... I tell all my managers, hire for attitude – because you know you can't buy attitude, you can't train attitude."
—CNBC's Ying Shan Lee contributed to this article.

articles.title: Singapore PM Wong rejects weaker currency as shortcut to competitiveness
articles.text:
SINGAPORE — Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong pushed back against the idea of weakening the Singapore dollar to boost competitiveness, saying the city-state must instead rely on its economic strengths even as a strong currency adds to costs for businesses.
Wong said Singapore could continue to expect a strong and stable currency if its economy performs well, emphasizing its role in containing imported inflation.
"You're surely not suggesting that we depress our exchange rate in order to be more competitive," Wong said in a lighthearted exchange with DBS CEO Tan Su Shan at the bank's Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday.
His remarks came after Tan highlighted Singapore's reputation as a safe haven, which has helped attract capital and support the local currency, while acknowledging that the city-state remains a relatively expensive place to do business.
"The MAS will exercise monetary policy independently. The Singapore dollar will reflect our economic fundamentals, and if the economy does well, then we can continue to expect a strong, stable Sing dollar that is anchored on fundamentals and will also help keep imported inflation down," Wong said.
Unlike most major central banks, which primarily use interest rates to manage monetary conditions, the Monetary Authority of Singapore conducts policy through the exchange rate.
It manages the Singapore dollar against a basket of currencies belonging to the country's major trading partners, allowing the exchange rate to fluctuate within an undisclosed policy band.
The approach reflects Singapore's heavy dependence on international trade and imports, making currency movements particularly important for domestic prices.
A stronger Singapore dollar helps cushion the cost of imported goods and services, particularly during periods of elevated global inflation. But it can also make Singapore-produced goods and services more expensive for overseas buyers, adding pressure on exporters.
The Singapore dollar has strengthened almost 0.4% against the greenback since the start of the year.
Wong acknowledged those trade-offs, saying businesses would have to account for currency strength alongside Singapore's other operating costs.
"Companies that seek to export will have to factor that into the cost of doing business, together with the other costs that they experience in Singapore, as we all know, we are certainly not the cheapest location in Southeast Asia," he said.
Singapore strategy
Still, Wong argued that competing on price alone was not a viable strategy for Singapore, which must instead differentiate itself through its capabilities, stability and predictability.
"Companies are not looking for the cheapest locations," he said. "They are looking for capabilities. They are looking for stability. They are looking for predictability."
Wong also said Singapore could not compete on cost alone, and was instead developing broader industrial ecosystems linking multinational corporations, domestic suppliers, research capabilities and skilled workers.
Singapore's competitiveness ultimately depended on the value it offered businesses rather than its relative cost advantage, he added.
"We have to again play to our strengths and compete on the basis of the value we bring to the table," he said.

articles.title: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: How a gold-buying spree helps the yuan go global
articles.text:
Hi, this is Evelyn, writing to you from Beijing. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what I'm seeing and hearing from local businesses.
Buying gold every month for nearly two years is just part of China's plan to narrow a gap with the U.S. on holdings of the precious metal. What does that do to the yuan?
The big story
China's decades-long push for yuan internationalization is getting a lift from the buildout of Hong Kong as a gold trading center — denominated in the Chinese currency.
"As those trading volumes grow, there would be a growing volume of the physical gold trade that is denominated in RMB and not linked in USD," said Charles Chang, managing director and Greater China country lead for corporate ratings at S&P Global Ratings.
The Chinese yuan, also known as the renminbi, accounts for a fraction of international transactions in a global financial system dominated by the U.S. dollar. Analysts I spoke with don't expect major changes to that dynamic anytime soon, but Beijing's gold purchases and Hong Kong trading platform are just the latest steps toward supporting greater use of the yuan globally.
"The challenge with internationalizing the RMB it's somewhat more challenging to find places where you can use the RMB," Chang said. "In terms of gold particularly, if the RMB that the buyer receives can be converted to gold, then it gives more channels for the spending to be done."
Hong Kong, home to one of the world's largest stock exchanges, last month confirmed its efforts to develop a yuan-denominated gold market.
In a major move last year, the special administrative region of China linked its gold vault with one in Shanghai, allowing physical gold delivery to international institutions in Hong Kong denominated in yuan.
Over the next three years, Hong Kong plans to expand the capacity of its Shanghai-linked gold vault from 150 tonnes to over 2,000 tonnes, S&P's Chang pointed out.
That's nearly as large as all the gold reserves in China, he added. "If Hong Kong is able to complete this transaction, then it would become of the largest gold trading centers in the world."
U.S. dollar challenge
The U.S. still has the largest gold reserves in the world at over 8,100 tonnes, according to World Gold Council figures for the second quarter. China held about one-third of that at over 2,300 tonnes.
"China's 23-month gold buying streak reinforces the credibility of the renminbi's internationalization drive," said Hao Zhou, head of research and chief economist at Guotai Junan International in Hong Kong.
"By steadily increasing gold reserves, Beijing is strengthening the long-term backing of its financial system and reducing reliance on dollar-denominated reserve assets," he said. "While gold alone will not determine the RMB's global role, it enhances confidence in the currency and supports broader efforts to expand its use in trade, investment and official reserves."
Gold accumulation by China and other countries' central banks will help reduce global reliance on U.S. Treasurys and U.S. dollar reserves, said Xia Yingying, head of the precious metals and new energy research group, at Hangzhou-based Nanhua Futures. That's according to a CNBC translation of the Chinese.
"This will suppress the U.S. dollar's premium from being a core reserve currency, and raise the risk premium associated with the dollar regarding credit, fiscal policy and sanctions," Xia said. "In the medium to-long-term it will gradually weaken the U.S. dollar's monopolistic position in the global reserve system."
China's growing gold purchases, however, also come as U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday named gold-standard supporter Judy Shelton as a senior advisor focused on China.
The Asian economy's rise as a manufacturing powerhouse benefited from the U.S. decision to abandon the gold standard more than 50 years ago. "With the delinking of the dollar and gold, and the consequent rise in the oil price, western manufacturing became less economic, and capital went to Asia in search of cheap labor and overall lower costs," wrote the central bank research group OMFIF in 2021.
While China is the largest consumer and producer of gold, it is just one of many developing economies that has expanded its reserves since 2022, according to S&P. The World Gold Council showed Poland has increased its gold reserves by more tonnes than China.
Going to the source
The trend goes beyond financial transactions. Like with rare earths, Beijing's gold ambitions start with control of some of the product.
China has acquired major gold mines across Latin America, Africa and Asia, according to S&P Global Ratings.
"China's plans for gold and its activities in gold are comprehensive and long lasting. These trends are going to be in place for a number of years," Chang said.
"The comprehensive nature of this," he said, "is something that markets often miss."
Need to know
DeepSeek considers doubling latest funding round to up to $15 billion, sources say
China's DeepSeek is considering expanding its latest funding round to as much as 100 billion yuan ($14.9 billion), double its earlier target, with state-backed funds and corporate investors jostling for stakes, people familiar with the matter told CNBC. AI startup Manus raises $500 million from IDG Capital and others, indicating investors aren't deterred by Beijing's unprecedented order to block Meta's short-lived $2 billion acquisition.

European trade commissioner Maroš Sefčovič said Friday that China has agreed to halve its exports of hybrid cars to the bloc. China's auto market is on track for its worst year since 2021, with sales down by more than 20% over roughly the first three quarters of the year, according to China Passenger Car Association data as of Sept. 27.
After a yearslong slump, China's real estate market may be set for a turnaround
Residential real estate prices may hit a bottom in the third quarter of 2028, S&P Global Ratings said. It added that prices in China's largest cities, such as Beijing and Shanghai, will likely recover as soon as next year.

articles.title: Cramer's lightning round: 'I like BlackBerry very much'
articles.text:
Nokia: "They're doing AI fiber at the edge which is really good. And don't forget they took some money from Nvidia ... I think that they're actually a core component in the growth of the data center."
Applied Aerospace & Defense: "I like the stock. I don't think that it's warranted this decline. I would stick with the stock."

articles.title: GM CEO: We're making leaps and bounds toward 'eyes-off, hands-off' driving
articles.text:
General Motors CEO Mary Barra said Monday that the automaker remains on track to introduce "eyes-off, hands-off" driving technology by 2028.
GM announced last October that it plans to launch its next-generation driver-assistance system in the electric Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028 before expanding to other models. Unlike the company's existing Super Cruise system, which allows drivers to take their hands off the wheel but requires them to remain attentive, the new technology is designed to let drivers take their eyes off the road under certain conditions.
Barra told CNBC's Jim Cramer on "Mad Money" that she recently tested the technology and was impressed by how much it had improved since an earlier ride in March. "They're making so much progress on our goal to have eyes off, hands off in the '28 time frame," the CEO said. "We're going to be well positioned from a personal autonomy perspective." She added, "When people want to drive, they can. When they don't, they won't need to as that grows."
GM's push into personal autonomous driving follows its decision to exit its Cruise robotaxi business in December 2024 after spending more than $10 billion. Rather than compete in the increasingly crowded driverless ride-hailing market, the automaker redirected its resources toward developing autonomous systems for vehicles consumers own. "We're not in the taxi business. We're not in the bus business," Barra said.
She acknowledged that exiting the robotaxi market was difficult but defended the move, noting that GM retained much of the Cruise team to work on personal autonomous driving. "It was a tough decision, but I think it was the right decision," she said.
Barra also pushed back against the idea that widespread adoption of autonomous vehicles could eventually reduce the need for personal car ownership. She recalled earlier predictions that ride-hailing services such as Uber and Lyft would sharply reduce vehicle sales, something that never materialized because "people still value that it's in my driveway. I can go wherever I want, whenever I want."

articles.title: Jim Cramer says the bull market's remarkable 4-year run offers a crucial lesson for investors
articles.text:
The stock market has given investors plenty of reasons to sell over the past four years. CNBC's Jim Cramer said those who resisted the temptation have reaped the rewards.
Since bottoming on Oct. 12, 2022, the S&P 500 has surged roughly 118%, weathering aggressive Federal Reserve rate hikes, a banking crisis, sweeping tariffs and a war in Iran. The rally began amid widespread pessimism about inflation and the economy, yet none of those setbacks managed to derail it.
"The real lesson is that there never seems to be a good time to invest, because bad things do happen quite regularly, and yet investing is a superior way to get a return," the "Mad Money" host said.
The gains have been substantial.
According to Cramer, a $10,000 investment in the S&P 500 at the October 2022 bottom would now be worth nearly $23,061. Some of the market's biggest winners delivered even greater returns. Nvidia surged roughly 1,875% over that period, turning a $10,000 investment into approximately $197,505. A $10,000 investment in Meta Platforms would have grown to more than $58,800 as shares climbed 488%. Cramer's Charitable Trust, the portfolio run by CNBC's Investing Club, owns shares of Nvidia and Meta.
For Cramer, the bigger takeaway isn't about picking the next market leader. It's about staying invested through uncertainty rather than trying to time every downturn and recovery.
"We could not have predicted either the big declines or the big rebounds," Cramer said. "We could've turned tail so many times in these four years. And we would've been all the poorer for it."
Cramer talked further about why he always stays in the market in his Sunday column for Investing Club members. Club analyst Zev Fima wrote a follow-up story Monday, using an investment calculator that you can plug your own numbers into to show the power of compound interest.
The cost of missing a market rally can be substantial.
According to JPMorgan, an investor who put $10,000 into the S&P 500 and missed its 10 best trading days between 2005 and 2024 would have ended up with less than half the wealth of someone who stayed fully invested.
"Stay in, keep buying, don't lose faith," Cramer said. "Those are the lessons from this indomitable four-year-old bull market."

articles.title: S&P 500 futures are flat ahead of bank earnings; South Korea's Kospi falls below 6,000: Live updates
articles.text:
Futures tied to the broad market S&P 500 were little changed on Monday night, with traders bracing for a slew of corporate earnings reports from major companies such as JPMorgan Chase and UnitedHealth.
S&P 500 futures inched down about 0.1%, while Nasdaq-100 futures lost 0.2%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures rose 17 points.
In Asia, South Korea's benchmark Kospi fell more than 6%, dropping below 6,000 to its lowest level since July 31, while the small-cap Kosdaq fell 4.23%. Japan's Nikkei 225 declined 2.63% and the Topix slipped 0.49%. Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 was 0.29% lower.
Big banks JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo are slated to release their results before the open on Tuesday. Dow member UnitedHealth is also on deck.
The early reports could set the tone for an earnings season with lofty expectations. Analysts on average expect S&P 500 profits grew by nearly 30% from the year-earlier period, according to FactSet.
"Three groups will likely shape how investors read the season: 1) Banks (consumer and business health), 2) Big Tech (AI monetization), and 3) Energy (the durability of oil-driven profits)," wrote Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise. "Underneath these areas, the health of consumers and businesses amid higher interest rates, elevated costs, and concerns about the macroeconomic environment will be closely monitored across sectors throughout the season."
Investors on Tuesday will also parse through existing home sales figures along with commentary from Federal Reserve officials Christopher Waller, Tom Barkin and Susan Collins.
Later in the week, inflation data for September will be released – which could jolt Treasury yields after they reached multidecade highs recently. The U.S. bond market was closed Monday due to the Indigenous Peoples' Day holiday.
Wall Street is coming off a mixed session. The Dow ended Monday more than 195 points higher, while declines in memory stocks pushed the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 into negative territory for the day.

articles.title: Elon Musk gives $276 million to Republican groups, becomes biggest known 2026 midterm donor
articles.text:
Elon Musk spent more than $276 million in newly disclosed donations to Republican groups since July, making him the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterm election as the party fights to hold its majorities in Washington this November.
The largest share – $158 million – went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing Republican Senate candidates, according to figures provided by Musk's representatives to The New York Times and confirmed Monday to CNBC by Lindsey Curnutte, a spokesperson for Musk's America PAC.
The Tesla and SpaceX CEO also gave more than $76 million to America PAC, the group he founded during the 2024 election, which has built a large voter-turnout operation in competitive Senate and House races.
The new contributions bring Musk's known federal political giving for the 2025-26 cycle to roughly $366 million, already surpassing the approximately $290 million he spent during the 2024 presidential election. The scale of the latest giving is historic: Musk's $158 million contribution to Senate Leadership Fund is among the largest known political donations by an individual in U.S. history.
The new figures were disclosed days ahead of a Thursday Federal Election Commission filing deadline, when political committees are due to report their third-quarter finances.
The Senate Leadership Fund has spent heavily this cycle to defend the Republican majority, including in Texas, where GOP Attorney General Ken Paxton is running against Democrat James Talarico. Talarico leads Paxton 48.4% to 45.0% in FiftyPlusOne's polling average as of Oct. 12.
Musk separately gave $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, which supports Paxton. He also contributed $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the leading super PAC supporting House Republicans, $10 million to the Republican Governors Association and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association, the Times reported and Curnutte confirmed.
The trillionaire's footprint in Texas has expanded rapidly in recent years, with Tesla, X and The Boring Company now headquartered in the state and SpaceX growing its manufacturing and launch operations there.
The political spending is also a sharp reversal from Musk's public comments last year.
"In terms of political spending, I'm going to do a lot less in the future," Musk said in May 2025.
At the time, Musk was stepping back after a highly visible role in President Donald Trump's administration and a public falling-out with the president. The two have since repaired their relationship, appearing together at several recent events.
Musk also retains deep ties to the federal government through SpaceX, a major NASA and Pentagon contractor. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last month also named him co-director of Project Meridian, a Pentagon panel studying the future of warfare.
— Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump 'not happy' with Kimberly Guilfoyle, weighs firing her as ambassador to Greece
articles.text:
President Donald Trump said Monday that he is "not happy" with Kimberly Guilfoyle, and is considering whether to fire her as U.S. ambassador to Greece.
Trump's comments at the White House after a series of critical articles in The Wall Street Journal about Guilfolye's conduct before and after she became ambassador.
Asked by a reporter if he was weighing firing Guilfolye, Trump replied, "Well, we're looking at it."
"Yeah, we're not happy," the president said.
Guilfoyle previously was engaged to Trump's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. After the couple broke up, the president appointed the former Fox News personality as ambassador.
CNBC has requested comment from Guilfoyle's attorney about Trump's remark.
The Journal on Sept. 25 published an article under the headline, "The Mystery Man Shadowing Kimberly Guilfoyle as She Pushes Deals Across Europe."
The story detailed Guilfoyle's push to get U.S. allies in Eastern Europe to buy billions of dollars of American natural gas.
The article said that Guilfoyle told people who were the targets of her effort that "they should deal with a Greek construction firm called Aktor Group, a newcomer to the gas business that had teamed up with a Greek state-backed energy company to bring in liquefied natural gas from the U.S."
The article detailed how Guilfoyle had traveled frequently with a top lobbyist for Aktor named Christos Marafatsos, who has been "joining her for meetings at her ambassadorial residence and with government officials in countries around the region—a highly unusual move for a private citizen."
On Oct. 7, the Journal published an article detailing how Guilfoyle allegedly asked a Trump donor named Eric Deters in July 2025 to pay $100,000 for what she said was an American Express bill before her upcoming Senate confirmation hearing for the ambassadorship.
A lawyer for Guilfoyle told the newspaper that Deters owed her a balance for "traveling to and supporting" events where she was hired to speak.
On Saturday, the Journal published another article that said during the January 2026 World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, she had "boasted ... about her close ties to two Greek tycoons and said they were bankrolling her high-rolling trips around the world."
In a statement on Sunday, Guilfoyle's lawyers "denied she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from the Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid," The Associated Press reported.
The lawyers "also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle's travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she 'sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department's travel regulations,' " The AP reported, citing the statement.

articles.title: Here's a calculator to explain why Cramer always stays invested. Plug in your own numbers, too
articles.text: In his Sunday column this week, Jim Cramer noted that this market is facing several headwinds — both at home and abroad. So many, in fact, that he was having a hard time making a case for owning stocks, at least for now. And yet, Jim won't skip his monthly contribution to his S & P 500 index fund and go to cash. "I invest knowing that, as crazy as it has been, I have made a lot of money with stocks," Jim wrote. "And as crazy as it might be, I believe I can do so again." The reason it works comes down to two words: Compound interest. Small, consistent gains over time, compounded through regular contributions, can supercharge your wealth. It's all about time spent in the market, not about trying to time it. Here's an example: Start with a balance of 0. Make a $100 contribution to your 401(k) plan or an index fund at the end of every month. Use a 40-year investment horizon; that's most of a person's working life. Assume a 10% per year rate of return (compounded annually), roughly the gain for the S & P 500 over the past three decades, before accounting for inflation. Over the 40-year period, or 480 months, you would have invested $48,000. However, thanks to the power of compounding, you would actually have over $555,000 sitting in your account. Compounding starts slowly before it really ramps up as the percentage gains are realized on increasingly large numbers. Thus, the term compounding refers to the most recent gain compounding on top of all the gains that came before it. That's why it's so important to start young. The earlier you start, the more time you have to realize the power of compounding. That's especially true when it comes to retirement planning. Note how the blue bars increase at a constant pace over the years. That is simply the principal you've put in — $100 per month or $1,200 per year, consistently. The green bars, however, are where the real money is made: that's the interest you generate each year, and we see those bars, stacked on top of the principal, growing larger and larger each year at an exponential rate. The reason it works this way is that every time an interest payment comes due, it is paid from a large base. Imagine we have $100 invested at 10% per year (no additional payments). In the first year, we would generate $10 (10% of $100), leaving us with $110 at the end of the year, a $10 increase. In the second year, we generate another 10%, this time on the $110 we have sitting there. That adds $11 to the account (10% of $110), bringing our new total to $121 by the end of year two. The third year would be 10% of $121, or $12.10. As you can see, each year the interest payment grows slightly. Over time, that growth becomes massive, especially when you're adding money to the account along the way. Understanding and harnessing the power of compound interest is the key to financial freedom. This is not financial wizardry, nor does it require huge returns. It simply requires a disciplined savings plan, consistent investing, and trust in the process. That's just one scenario. Go back up and put your own numbers in the tool . Maybe you have a shorter time horizon to retirement. Maybe you are more conservative in your investment style and figure on a lower rate of return. CNBC's data and visualization team has created this investment growth calculator. All you have to do is provide four key assumptions: starting account value, monthly payment amount, assumed average annual rate of return, and investment horizon in years. The calculator does the rest, showing you how much money you've actually contributed (principal) and what the power of compounding can do to it over time (interest). articles.title: Hoàng Đức về quê bán trà sữa
articles.text:
Hoàng Đức về quê bán trà sữa
Không những bán trà sữa mà Hoàng Đức còn sơ hở là tiểu phẩm nữa.
Trên sân cỏ, các cầu thủ nổi tiếng thường xuất hiện với quần đùi, áo số, tập trung cao độ trong từng pha bóng. Nhưng rời xa những trận đấu căng thẳng, nhiều người lại có cuộc sống đời thường giản dị, gần gũi, thậm chí sẵn sàng nhập hội diễn tiểu phẩm cùng người thân. Tiền vệ Nguyễn Hoàng Đức (sinh năm 1998, Hải Phòng) là một trong số đó.
Mới đây, đoạn clip tiền vệ đứng bán trà sữa ở quê, tranh thủ quay video bắt trend thu hút sự chú ý.
(Nguồn: @nguynhiyn81)
Trong khoảnh khắc này, bối cảnh là một vị khách nói với Hoàng Đức: “Chồng chị hay ghen, không cho mua mấy quán có trai đẹp, nên chị mới hay mua quán em!”. Câu nói tưởng như đang giải thích lý do thường xuyên ghé quán, nhưng thực chất lại là màn cà khịa nhan sắc của chủ quán là không đẹp trai.
Nghe xong, Hoàng Đức lập tức thể hiện vẻ mặt giận dỗi ra mặt. Biểu cảm của anh chàng khiến tình huống càng thêm hài hước, nhất là khi người bị trêu lại là một cầu thủ vốn quen thuộc với người hâm mộ bóng đá Việt Nam vì vừa đá bóng hay vừa đẹp trai.
“Em thích cái biểu cảm này. Nhưng mặt anh Đức giống đang ngủ ngon bị gọi dậy bán hàng á”, “Lỡ va vào ánh mắt phán xét của anh Đức”, “Chị nói thế là không được rồi chị khách ơi”, “Vừa kiêm tuyến giữa nay lại phải về bán trà sữa nữa. Ảnh sắp gánh GDP nước nhà rồi hả?”, “Chị khách nói thế nhiều người đau lòng lắm đấy ạ”, “Khách đi ra đây gặp em mình nói chút chuyện nhé!”,... là một số bình luận từ dân tình.
Thực tế, đây không phải công việc kinh doanh mới của Hoàng Đức. Quán trà sữa trong clip là của người em họ nam cầu thủ tại quê nhà Hải Phòng. Mỗi khi được nghỉ và trở về quê, nam cầu thủ thường ghé quán chơi, gặp gỡ người thân và bạn bè. Bởi vậy, hình ảnh Hoàng Đức đứng sau quầy trà sữa hay nhập vai trong những tiểu phẩm đời thường cũng không quá xa lạ với những người theo dõi anh.
Ngoài ra nhiều người cũng cho rằng khi về quê, Hoàng Đức có phần thoải mái hơn. Trái với vẻ tập trung trên sân cỏ hay sự kín tiếng trước truyền thông, ngoài đời, tiền vệ này không ngại trở thành nhân vật chính trong những màn trêu chọc qua lại với người thân.
Nguyễn Hoàng Đức sinh năm 1998, quê Hải Phòng, là một trong những tiền vệ nổi bật của bóng đá Việt Nam. Anh chàng bắt đầu bộc lộ năng khiếu bóng đá từ nhỏ, được tuyển chọn vào Trung tâm Đào tạo bóng đá trẻ Hải Dương khi học lớp 4. Năm 2017, Hoàng Đức gia nhập CLB Viettel, từng bước khẳng định tên tuổi và góp công giúp đội bóng vô địch V.League 2 năm 2018, V.League 1 năm 2020. Từ tháng 10/2024 đến nay, Hoàng Đức thi đấu cho CLB Ninh Bình.
Ở cấp độ đội tuyển, anh từng cùng U20 Việt Nam tham dự World Cup U20 năm 2017, giành 2 HCV tại SEA Games 30 và 31, 2 lần cùng tuyển Việt Nam vô địch ASEAN Cup (2024 và 2026),... trở thành nhân tố quan trọng của đội tuyển quốc gia. Hoàng Đức cũng từng 3 lần giành danh hiệu Quả bóng Vàng Việt Nam. Gần nhất, Hoàng Đức đảm nhận vai trò đội trưởng ĐTQG Việt Nam tại FIFA ASEAN Cup 2026.
Bên cạnh sự nghiệp sân cỏ, Hoàng Đức cũng được cho là sở hữu khối tài sản nổi bật. Năm 2021, anh xây nhà cho bố mẹ ở quê, đóng góp phần lớn chi phí theo thông tin được bài viết đề cập. Cuối năm 2025, nam cầu thủ hoàn thành căn hộ riêng rộng gần 120 m² tại khu vực Mỹ Đình, Hà Nội.
(Tổng hợp)
